WARBURTON (Queens, Prince Edward Island) moved that the Public Accounts for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1909, and volumes I. and III. 'of the report of the Auditor General for the same period, be referred to the Committee on Public Accounts.
Mr. HAUGHTON LENNOX (South Sim-coel. Before that motion is put I wish to direct the attention of this House to the advisability of making some change in our method of procedure in the Public Accounts Committee. There is no member of this House, whether he be a member of the Public Accounts Committee or not, who has not some knowledge of the very great difficulty experienced in getting at the information which the public of this country require in relation to the Public Accounts of Canada. There is no member of this House who. aside from political considerations, would hesitate to admit that in certain cases our investigations are not as full as thev ought to be and that we do not get at the true state of the facts to

the extent we should. The opposition which we who investigate axe met with [DOT]from time to time by certain gentlemen in the House is one conspicuous cause of the failure to elicit the facts. In the years that have gone by it is true we have been able to divulge very startling conditions in reference to the public expenditure of Canada, but I venture to think, and I believe most people in Canada who follow the trend of public affairs think, that we are only on the threshold of all that could be divulged did we have the proper facilities to elicit it. I would be glad to feel-and for the present I will assume, and the subsequent attitude which the government takes will show whether I am justified or not- I would be glad to feel that the government is as anxious as are the members of the opposition that full light should be thrown on the circumstances surrounding the expenditure of public moneys. Following a time honoured precedent the hon. gentleman (Mr. Warburton) has to-day moved that the Public Accounts and 'the Auditor General's Report for the year ending March 31 be referred to the Public Accounts Committee for investigation.
Now, what I propose, Mr. Speaker, is that we 'should have a wider range; that instead of referring the public accounts merely for the year ending the 31st March last and the Auditor General's Report for the same period, we should Tefer at least two ; years of the public accounts to that committee. I do this for various reasons, one of which is that it is the Public Accounts and the Auditor General's Report for the year ending 31st March last which give the true bearing of certain items in the accounts of the year preceding. Therefore as it should be the object of every member of this House to get at the true state of the facts in the most expeditious manner possible, it is important that we should be able, after these accounts have come in, to go back to the preceding year and avail ourselves of the information afforded by the subsequent transactions in connection with the same item. We cannot close our eyes to the fact that many hon. gentlemen who believe they -are acting in the interest of their party set themselves deliberately to block the investigation which is going on, impelled by the belief that if they can prevent it for one year it will be dropped altogether. The matter comes up within a few weeks of prorogation, and they will not allow the investigation to proceed rapidly; they take all the technical and captious objections possible, with the result that very little information is elicited during the balance of the session; and when we come to another session we are confronted with the statement: You cannot go into that, because the only public accounts referred to the committee are those of the year ended the 31st of March last. If the public ac-Mr. LENNOX.
counts of the two years w7ere referred, to the committtee, we would not be met with that difficulty, because these hon. gentlemen would realize, contrary to what they believe now, that we could not be blocked altogether in our investigations. It may be suggested that it would be rather unfortunate if the committee went back to investigate not the public accounts of last year, but those of the year before. To that I reply that no hon. member of this House is going to ask the committee to investigate for two years back, unless there is some good reason for doing it. It is said that there are no birds in last year's nests, and we realize that in the majority of cases our best work is done on the recent accounts; but there are a great many cases in which light can be thrown on a transaction on which the public should be informed if the rule did not confine us to one year's accounts, but gave us liberty to investigate the accounts ot two years. I had intended to move an amendment to this motion, but I have decided not to do so on this occasion. I have listened, not always with approval, to the remarks of hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to long sessions. I have tried to believe, but have not succeeded in believing, that these hon. gentlemen are sincere in the ideas which suggest these remarks. Any one who reads the records of this House will, on a careful study of this matter, come to the conclusion, that the evidence is not strong that the government is sincere in desiring short sessions. If we want to have short sessions combined with efficiency of investigation, we will adopt the suggestion I make. If hon. gentlemen desire to have the time of the Public Accounts Committee used to advantage, and a rule broad enough to enable us to work effectively without having to make special applications to the House, they will agree to the suggestion I make, and say that in years to come, as long at any rate as this government is in power-and I think I can promise that when we get into power in the near future, we shall be quite willing to continue the rule-we shall have the right, without making any special motion in the House, to investigate the public accounts and the Auditor General's Report for at least two years whenever any hon. gentleman of this House deems it in the public interest that such an investigation should be made.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend has not made any motion on the subject proposed, it is not necessary for me to discuss the matter at length. The impressions I have received of the Public Accounts Committee are not the same as those which my hon. friend seems to entertain. I think that those who have given the closest attention to the Public Accounts Committee will be able to testify th^t the

investigations of that committee are very thorough, and they take a very wide range. If one wanted to be critical, he could often complain that the committee enters into the consideration of matters which strictly speaking do not pertain to its duties at all. But on a question of that character it is well to take a very liberal view not to be too technical. Inasmuch as we have annual parliaments, it follows that there should be annual inquiries into the public accounts. These matters are all regulated by the long experience of the mother of parliaments, and the rules and practices found to be successful in the mother country may safely, in most instances, be continued here. I quite understand that there may be cases in which the events of one year may be closely connected to those of another; the transaction beeinning in one year may extend into another year. In cases of that kind it would not be unreasonable that the whole transaction should be reviewed, and I am sure that the Public Accounts Committee would at all times be willing to grant such an investigation. If there be any special circumstances which seem to call for such an inquiry, I think we can safely trust in the future as in the past the wisdom of the Public Accounts Committee and ultimately the wisdom of the House of Commons. It is unfortunate that in the discussion of questions in that committee occasionally some party feeling may be manifested on one side or on the other; a man who has strong party views may sometimes think that a man who has strong party views on the other side is a little unreasonable. We must learn to make allowance for one another in these things. 1 am persuaded that, all in all, the work of the Public Accounts Committee is well done; and if it should be desired at any time to inquire into a matter that is not before the committee in the usual formal way, I am sure that the committee and the House of Commons itself will always, on a statement of the facts, be prepared to provide a remedy.

I would like to say a word in support of what the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) has said. My experience of the Public Accounts Committee differs entirely from that of the Minister of Finance; and when he invokes the example of the mother of parliaments, my hon. friend cannot ignore the fact that the investigation of the public accounts is very differently conducted in the mother country. In England, under the rules of the House, the Public Accounts Committee is composed of eleven of or at most fifteen members of the House. The chairman is always by custom a member of the opposition. It would be entirely unheard of in England that one of the members of the committee, desiring
infox'mation on some particular transaction, would be opposed by a member of the same committee on legal technicalities. The thing has never occurred, and never could occur there, because the idea that dominates the Committee of Public Accounts in the British parliament is that any man can ask any question which may lead him to a full understanding of the transaction under consideration. But what do we find here? So far from exhibiting any wisdom, the proceedings in the Public Accounts Committee, during the past four or five years, have degenerated into a farce. People go there just to see the kind of a battle that is carried on, just to hear the objections made and the difficulties put in the way of getting any information on any transaction. I appeal to any hon. gentleman who has attended any of the meetings, if that be not the case. That committee is the place where it is most difficult to get any information. What usually happens? A number of gentlemen, who form part of the committee, come to the meeting, and a certain number do not find a single matter to investigate. It is but fair to presume therefore that they are satisfied with the accounts presented to them. They do not ask any questions, but are perfectly content. Other members come there who are not so easily pleased. Certain transactions have come under their observations on which they desire to be informed, and they call for the papers. These are brought down, and on looking over them, these members of the committee find reasons for pushing their researches a little further. Witnesses are then brought before the committee, but the minute you begin to examine them, other members of the committee, who 'seldom come there, who have asked for no papers, who presumably are satisfied with everything, make their appearance on such occasions, and make it their business to enter objections and prevent the investigation. Is that the case or is it not? Some four or five members, in some cases more, troop into that Public Accounts Committee room for the sole object of blocking the investigation. There can be no doubt about that. The best proof is that these gentleman, as a rule, are able lawyers, and they interpose objections just as they would in a court of law. An hon. member from Nova Scotia will base his objection upon the rules of investigation which obtain in his particular province. Other members from other provinces will make objections founded on rules of evidence which govern in their respective provinces. The result is you cannot proceed. If the case be one which seems to lead up to discoveries of irregularities, the stronger are the objections and the greater is the number of members who come in to support them. It seems to me that proceeds from an entire mis-

conception of the duties of that committee. There is no possible ground, I submit, on which one hon. member can object to another obtaining information, unless the latter ill-treats the witness or clearly wishes to obstruct the work of the committee, but when he puts a question to a witness with regard to a fact, is it tolerable that one of his colleagues should object because that question violates some rule of evidence in some provincial court, For instance, the objection will be urged that you cannot put that question unless you have a commencement of proof in writing or some other absolutely technical objection, which could only be made in a court of law. We have all seen some particular member apparently designated as being an able lawyer accustomed to cross-examine,, come into that committee when there is some ticklish matter under investigation, involving irregular transactions on the part of the government. We have seen four or five such members come there and sedulously one after another, object to questions on some technical rule of evidence. All members of parliament are not lawyers, and it is quite clear that this group of members has for its object the blocking of evidence and the preventing of our obtaining that information which the committee ou^ht to have. I am very glad that my hon. friend from Simcoe has brought that matter to the notice of the House. It has been noticed by all strangers and witnesses attending the committee, and the result is that the examination before that committee, instead of being serious, becomes a farce.

I am very much surprised at the statements of the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). If these came from other members of the opposition, I would say that they were drawing upon their imaginations, but my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), I think, is the last person who ought to complain of the treatment he has received from the Public Accounts Committee. I have been rather a regular attendant at the meetings of that committee during the past three or four sessions
Hear, hear.
And I challenge the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) to point out one specific case in which he ever asked a proper question for proper information and failed to have that question allowed.

I may say that I have not asked many questions altogether in the Public Accounts Committee. and I do not recollect that my hon. friend ever interrupted me, and I would not be particular Mr. MONK.
if he did, because I am able to fight my way, but I have heard, on many occasions, objections made on technical grounds to questions put.

I knew that the hon. gentleman could not point to one instance when he put a proper question and it was objected to. But let me point out what has occasioned this irritation on the part of the hon. members for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) and others of their friends. In the first place, they ask for the papers and the original papers are brought down. Then they ask that witnesses be summoned; and to the best of my recollection, there never has been a refusal to bring witnesses from any part of the country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Thousands and tens of thousands of dollars have been squandered bringing witnesses, who, not only could not give any information, but who, I believe, these gentlemen knew could not give any; but they brought them because they had some ulterior object in view. After asking a few questions regarding the item under discussion, they drift off to some other outside matter, and when members of the committee who have some regard for the rules of order and decency

Oh, oh.
Mr. CARVELL-attempt to hold them down to the question under discussion, these gentlemen make the charge that an attempt is being made to burk the investigation. Let them ask for their witnesses, and confine themselves to the subject matter under investigation and I can promise, as far as I am concerned, that they will meet with no difficulty, and I challenge them to point out where I or any other member, in the past four sessions, have attempted to obstruct investigation into any particular subject before the committee.
I am very glad this matter has come up. These accusations have been hurled at members on this side of the House from one end of Canada to the other. And I may say that my own name has been bandied about from the Atlantic to the Pacific as one of the leaders of a dark lantern brigade. I have only to repeat that I have not a word to take back that I have ever uttered in that committee. I have never objected to a solitary question that was proper;-I do not mean technically proper; I am not talking along the line of whether a question is one that would be allowed in a court of law or not; I mean a question bearing on the subject at issue. If these hon. gentlemen opposite will direct their investigations to the subject under discussion and not to some extrinsic matter they will have no difficulty. But I am afraid that if they continue to carry out the policy they have

pursued in the past, of attempting to bring out matters that have nothing to do with the subject under discussion, if they will attempt to use the Public Accounts Committee and the money of Canada as a means of trying to get some information which they think may possibly be of benefit to them in their constituencies but has nothing to do with the subject of the investigation, they will meet with the same treatment that they have met with in the past and of which they are complaining here to-day. We might as well have a clear understanding on this point. As a matter of fact, so far as I, for one, am concerned, there has been no objection in the past, and will be no objection in the future, to any proper investigation; every subject can be laid as bare as it possibly can be laid. On the other hand, I can only warn hon. members that if they will attempt to use this power of investigation in a way in which they are not entitled to use it, I am afraid they will meet with the same treatment as in the past.

I do not desire to occupy the time of the House in repeating what other gentlemen have said on this very important subject. I think (that, especially seeing that we have a new chairman, not so much accustomed as others to our ways, even what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has said, may do a great deal of good. I can say that I have nothing to complain of particularly myself; but I have again and again in that committee heard gentlemen who are not versed in the methods and forms of the law, attempting to ask a question of a witness, a perfectly proper question, when three or four gentlemen would at once spring to their feet objecting that the question was not put in proper form. There is not a member of that committee who hears me but knows that that is the case. The hon. member for Carleton, N. B., (Mr. Carvell) asked the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) to give an instance. I can give him a very common instance of most outrageous interference with the witnesses, i have myself, again and again, in examining witnesses as to the value of property which they have sold to the government, asked them, as the very best test of that value, what they had paid for the property, which, perhaps, they had bought within a month and may not even have paid for; and everybody knows who is on that committee who the gentlemen were who objected that this was an attempt to compel a man to disclose his private business. The hon. member (Mr. Carvell) will not deny this-
Will the hon. member name a specific instance; I cannot recall such a thing.
Oh, oh.
I would like to have an instance.
There are so many that it is quite unnecessary-
Oh, oh.
One case was brought before the House.
What was it?

That is quite enough; I will not give names unnecessarily; I know what I am talking about, and I do not think that there is one of the gentlemen here who has been declaiming but knows that I have only stated the facts. We have investigated the prices of articles sold to the government where we know that the most extravagant prices have been paid. I have asked what the seller paid for it, and what was his reply? His reply, suggested by a member of the committee, was that that was prying into a man's private business. I have even heard the chairman say that the witness was not bound to answer. Is that decent? Is that right? Is that reasonable, fair investigation? The hon. member (Mr. Carvell) knows that for a whole week we struggled with one witness to make him produce his invoices. He refused. We, at last, put him in a position where he would be forced to produce them, and then he said they were burnt. And we had to bring a man all the way from Galt, Ontario, to tell us at what price he sold these articles to the witness when the witness might have told us at once. I have heard members, not of the legal profession, asking a witness questions who were persist-tently interrupted by some legal gentlemen until the witness, alive to what was going on, found in what he should be careful, and then we might as well abandon the investigation. That is a very common thing, and every member of that committee knows it. As I have said, however, I think this little discussion will do good. It tends to show the absurdity of pretending that this is a court of inquiry to be conducted according to legal procedure. It is an investigation of business questions by business men, and ought to be carried on in the way in which business men would investigate such questions in their own office.

As one member of that committee, for some time past I have regarded it as of little value in ascertaining anything with regard to the expenditure of public money. There is hardly a layman in this House, except one or two, who would go before that committee to investigate any of the matters referred to, for we know from experience that as soon as it appears that information is being brought out of value to the country,



we are badgered by a number of lawyers in that committee under the plea that we are not following the procedure laid down for a court of law. These gentlemen seem to forget that the rules that apply in a court of law do not apply here. I am well within the mark when I say I have heard that plea raised a hundred times, and I have often seen fifteen or twenty minutes of the valuable time of that committee wasted in a discussion which finally resulted in the member being prevented from putting his question because it was not according to the rules of evidence in a court of law. And I do not know a much greater sinner in this respect than the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) says that the effort is to make the investigation thorough, and that it is thorough. It may be thorough as far as it goes, but, unfortunately, it does not go far enough. The time at the disposal of the committee is not sufficient to enable it to make a fair inquiry, by the examining of witnesses, when members are hampered in putting their questions. Of the thousands of items in the Auditor General's Report, only an extremely small proportion can be investigated owing to the absolute obstruction in that committee. That has been found to be the case over and over again. It may be said that if you go back over more than one year you even increase the number of subjects to he investigated. That is true. But one advantage of going back, as any one who has been in the House any considerable length of time will know, is that you may get most valuable information regarding these transactions after a year has passed. Generally, parties are close-mouthed for a year, but when they begin to settle up they are apt to be dissatisfied with one another and to disclose information which would not otherwise be in the possession of members or of this House. But, try to go hack into the previous public expenditures and you are met at once with the objection: 'You are going beyond the fiscal year.' That objection has been raised over and over again.
The members of the committee who have been endeavouring to get information have ' been prevented from getting it on that one ground alone, I do not'think that is right. I remember a long inquiry that took place in 1893, and when the then opposition desired to go back two years, the offer was made to them that they might go back two years, or three years, or four or five years, and they got that right. We said they had the right to go back just as far as they liked, only they would have to say that thev had reasonable grounds for suspicion that something was wrong; and if they desired to bring evidence with regard to anything that took place three or four years ago, we allowed that to be done. I Mr. SPROULE.
thought that was right. I always agreed with it when our friends were in power.
I think if there were not an effort made now to restrict the inquiry within the limit of one year, and that the last year, there would not be so much inclination to go back. But only in cases where there was a strong ground for suspicion that something could be got out which had not been brought to public attention, would any member of parliament desire to go back beyond a year. I think it would do a great deal of good if we had the right, though we might not exercise it very often. The Minister of Finance says: If you make certain allegations of fact the House will consent. Well, allegations of fact have been presented to that committee over and over again, and the committee did not consent; and I think in one or two cases when it was brought up in the House, the House did not consent. There is always some excuse made, so that no matter what you do you are confronted with obstruction, and you are prevented from doing what you conceive to be your duty. The hon. member opposite who just took his seat said that no proper question was ever refused. Well, what is meant by a proper question depends altogether on the mind of the gentleman who uses the word. If we were only to ask such questions as the hon. gentleman thought were proper questions, we would never bring out the information that we desired. Besides, one hon. gentleman might have something in his mind that others did not have, and he might desire to ask the question in a way that wrould bring out information which other hon. gentlemen could not bring out. I know that many laymen have been prevented from asking questions in the committee to such an extent that they have abandoned the attempt to go before that committee and endeavour to get any information, because of the way they are badgered by, I was going to say, the brigade of lawyers who have been constantly in the Public Accounts Committee session after session apparently to obstruct for many years past.

I beg to move the following amendment. [DOT]
That the motion now read be amended by inserting the words 'Public Accounts and Auditor General's Report for the fiscal year ending 31st March 1908' immediately after the word ' period ' in the said motion.
I have very little to add to wdiat has already been said, other than that it seems to me to be a very reasonable request on the part of my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) that the Public Accounts Committee should have an opportunity to investigate accounts further back in the history of this government than one

year. It is well known that it is only after a session commences that the Auditor General's Report is placed in the hands of members. Up to the present time we only have volume I. and volume III. of the Auditor General's Report, and I suppose it will be some days before we see volume II. That fact in itself is sufficient reason why the Public Accounts Committee should have an opportunity of investigating the Auditor General's Report after it has been in their hands for seven, or eight, or ten months.
My hon. friend from Carleton, New Brunswick, (Mr. Carvell) says that his name has been bandied from the Atlantic to' the Pacific ocean, to use his own words. If that is so, the reason is that my hon. friend has been the chief offender in the Public Accounts Committee, and if his name is well known from one end of this country to the other, as he states, it is because he has been most prominent among those who were unwilling to allow the opposition to investigate the public accounts of this government. Whether my hon. friend thinks that is an enviable reputation or not he must judge for himself. My hon. friend was asking for an example. I will give one. We had before the Public Accounts Committee the well known Mr. Mer-win, the great middleman who has been supplying the government with goods for many years. That gentleman was called before the committee and the question was put to him:	' How much did you pay for
these goods that were supplied to the government at such an enormous cost?' The gentleman supporting the government in the committee at once flew to his rescue and said:	'Don't answer the question.'
The chairman coincided, and the question was not answered then. But after my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup) summoned the gentleman who manufactured the goods, Mr. Willson, of Montreal, and after that gentleman came before the committee and was asked:	' What did you
supply these goods for to the general traders throughout the country?' and after he was compelled to answer that question, then the committee said:	'Oh, yes, Mr. Merwin can answer it now.' Now if there is any person in the House of Commons, or any member in the Public Accounts Committee, who, more than another, is responsible for the expenditure of large sums of money for bringing witnesses from different parts of the country, it is my hon. friend from Carleton, New Brunswick, he and his chief supporters in the committee. It is well known that one of the chief charges against this government is that they have .refused to the opposition members, and have refused to the people of Canada who are the taxpayers, such information as they are entitled to. That has been one of the chief charges against the govern-20i
ment for the last few years. Why is it that the government are afraid to let us- investigate the accounts that are two years old? If the public accounts are as fair as the government would lead this House to believe, then the Prime Minister himself should be the first man to stand up and say: This government is all right, we fear no investigation, let the opposition have all the latitude they want. We are not asking to investigate accounts ten years old; my hon. friend is only asking that accounts about two years old, should be brought before the committee for investigation. Surely that is a reasonable request, and if I am not mistaken, it is a request that the people of this country will endorse. I say that one of the principle charges against the government is that they are buying goods at enormous prices from middlemen, and the opposition are making an effort to investigate the charge in, some of the most glaring cases. My hon. friend from Carleton, New Brunswick* says if cases of this kind come up, perhaps, if you bring them before the committee, we may allow you to bring witnesses. Are we to be at the mercy of my hon. friend and his supporters in the committee? It is a well known fact that the committee is a partisan committee, the chairman is a supporter of the government, a large majority of the members of the committee are supporters of the government. If any man will look at the divisions in that committee during the last two years, he will find that when a question of this kind comes up, the supporters of the government on the committee, almost to a man, stand up and declare that these charges are too old and cannot be investigated. I am heartily in accord with my hon. friend's suggestion, and, therefore, I have the honour to present a motion which will give an opportunity to the Public Accounts Committee to make a fair and honest investigation of the public accounts of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, after the speech of my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), which I thought was on the whole very moderate, I did not expect my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) would move the amendment which he has just placed in your hands. I am unable to say at this moment whether this motion will toe acceptable to this House or whether it will not. I listened to the observations of my hon. friend -with some care, and I do not think I would object very seriously to the suggestion which he made to have the record of the accounts of the government for the last two years investigated. The matter is one which is quite worthy of consideration. I might say to my hon. friend, however, that he was a little more I -what shall I say?-previous than his

friend. If he had given us an opportunity to have looked at his motion, I do not think that we would have objected to it very seriously. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) observed that our procedure in the Public Accounts Committee was not on all fours with the example of the mother country. He stated that in the mother country the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee always belongs to the opposition. That is a practice which has never been followed in Canada as far as my memory goes. I am pretty sure that at confederation the practice was adopted which has prevailed ever since of selecting as chairman of the Public Accounts Committee a supporter of the government. There has been no departure from that principle. Perhaps it is regrettable in this matter we have not followed the example of the mother country. I think that we would do well, as far as we can, to conform our procedure to the rules which prevail in the mother land. But, perhaps my hon. friend will not have any objection if I ask him to allow this matter to stand so that we may consider this motion and perhaps we may come to an agreement upon it.

Mr. Speaker, 1 sincerely hope that the mover of this amendment will accept the suggestion made by the right hon. the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and allow this matter to stand in the hope that the government will accept the proposition. As I take the words of the right hon. gentleman as an indication that the government intend to look into this matter, I would venture to suggest that there is another matter that they might well consider in connection with the same committee. Whether the committee is to be allowed to go back two years or only one is a matter of comparatively little moment, but there does seem to me to be a matter of the utmost importance, the very basis upon which the committee works, and this may be an opportune time to have it decided what the real function of each member of that committee is. Without wishing to do anything more than to speak with perfect calmness upon the matter, I think that all members upon this side of the House will say that our chairman for the last term gave perfect satisfaction to this side of the House, both by his ability and integrity. Whenever papers have been moved for to be brought before the committee there has been no ground for complaint from this side of the House of any papers not being allowed to be obtained. As far as the subpoenaeing of witnesses is concerned, I do not think that primarily there is any ground for complaint by hon. members on this side of the House. So, Sir, a great deal of good can be done by the committee, and I ven-Kir WILFRID LATTRIER.
ture to think a great deal more might be done if one little change were made. When a matter is referred to the committee, prima facie, it being the Public Accounts Committee, every member of this House would have the same duty to perform; that is, to endeavour, if possible, to ascertain if the funds of the people have been properly or improperly spent. Nobody could have attended the meetings of that committee without having been struck by two facts; first, that no member of that committee has the slightest interest in investigating the payment of any of these accounts except members of the opposition. I quite admit that it would not altogether be natural for members of the government to be as suspicious as members of the opposition, but I think every one must admit- which casts a light upon the subsequent proceedings-that under no circumstances is any attempt made to investigate anything by any member of the House except by a member of the opposition. For this reason the whole committee is formed into two camps, and this does seem to be absolutely absurd' in a committee like the Public Accounts 'Committee.
There is no doubt that when this committee comes to the discharge of its duties it has one side-the opposition-trying to investigate and the other side-the government-trying to prevent investigation. It is all very well to find fault with this, that and the other thing, but there is the primary difficulty and so from day to day the opposition is prevented from making the investigation it desires to make. Let me give you a little illustration. We have the case occurring again and again when a matter has come before the committee. A question has been asked in the committee and it has been ruled that it has been improperly asked. A vote is taken in the committee and a report is asked for in order that the minority of the committee may appeal to this House, where hon. gentlemen are in the majority and where there is a ' Hansard ' in order that the matter may be threshed out whether the member of the opposition who asked the question was wrong or whether the supporters of the government who prevented it from being answered were wrong. Surely one would think there could be no conceivable objection to a question of that kind being referred to this House where hon. gentlemen opposite are in such a majority, yet the rule has been laid down again and again that we shall not be allowed the right of appeal from the Public Accounts Committee to this House unless the whole matter is closed, and that means that the party who has been unable to ask the question must drop that question and all other questions he wishes to ask in order to get an opportunity of finding out whether the primary question was correct or not.

Can any one imagine that any hon. gentleman who really desired to have a fair and honest investigation of the public accounts would impose such a condition upon men who were asking a question or who would say that you are bound by that question and that you shall not be allowed to appeal to the House of Commons unless, you drop your case and forego all other questions that you wish to ask? That is the greatest objection we have had in the committee and it does seem to me that there is no reason why we should not be allowed to appeal upon an interlocutory matter in the committee just as well as upon a final matter. Another difficulty that has arisen is that every witness practically that the opposition examines is an adverse witness. I do not suppose one would find one witness out of a hundred in the Public Accounts Committee who is not an adverse witness and that is a drawback to the opposition in its investigations.
What do you mean by an adverse witness?

Adverse to the party trying to investigate the accounts and bring out the facts as to the expenditure. In trying to find out whether the expenditure is honest or not the witness, in almost every case, is adverse to the crossexaminer because he wishes to prevent the facts being elicited. There is no disputing the fact that the great majority of witnesses are very able witnesses-exceedingly able witnesses-men who know the facts, who, in most cases, are interested in concealing the facts and men who are most competent to attain the object which they desire. If members sitting on the government side would help members on the opposition side to investigate these matters instead of helping to burk such, inquiry they would only be doing their full duty to the public. Instead of being hindered we should receive from them every possible assistance. How often does it happen, that in a case which it is in the interests of the people that the facts should be made known, the cross-examiner, when he begins to examine his witness, knows exactly how far his case will go, knows exactly what evidence he is to receive? It seems to me that if a member of this House is willing to spend the time that is necessary-and every one who has taken charge of such matters knows the long preparation necessary in investigation and inquiry-it does seem to me it would come with better grace from hon. gentlemen opposite if they would assist the member who is trying to do his duty instead of throwing obstacles in his way. I am prepared to support the amendment made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain), but I do hope the right hon. leader of the House will consider carefully the functions of this committee, and perhaps when we
get the new rules which are promised there may be one under which the work of the Public Accounts Committee will in the future be much more valuable than it has been in the past.

Whilst we are all in such an amicable mood maybe the House would listen for a moment to another suggestion which, not for the first time, I have to make, and indeed I am not sure that the first minister himself is not entirely in favour of it. I was glad to hear the remarks made by the Minister of Finance with reference to the reasonableness of the committee (and he was certain of the House) granting the committee back time so to speak, were it shown to be necessary in order to get at all the facts of the case; and also the position taken by the Prime Minister in thinking the suggestion made by my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) a reasonable one. The two great troubles that appear to be in the way of that committee doing the work it ought to do are these: in the first place the committee is too large to do good work. We assemble pretty nearly one half of the House of Commons there, fresh from all the disturbance and party rancour in the House and they immediately line themselves up on two sides, one side never making a move for the investigation of any of the items in the Public Accounts, and indeed watching very carefully and very jealously every move made by the opposition to examine into items, and using every reasonable and sometimes unreasonable method of making the inquiry as ineffective as possible, if not going further and preventing it altogether. Now, you will eliminate the greater part of that unreasonable party spirit on both sides by having a small committee and composing that committee chiefly of men of experience in Public Accounts, and in practical business work. Those are two elements which I think would make an effective committee. I am pretty certain that a committee of 15 members appointed in that way to investigate the Public Accounts would really do good work for the government as well as for the country. After all, it is not any gentleman's affairs that are being looked into; it is not the government's affairs that are being looked into except in so far as they are the supervisors of puhlic expenditure; it is the money of the whole country that has been expended and the whole country and every member of parliament should see to it that that money has been properly expended, or that the facts about its wrong expenditure should be disclosed. In the end nearly every government comes to its defeat- not so much through mistaken policies as through that dead weight growing every year of bad or foolish or corrupt expenditures. The government can have no better

friend than an intelligent and able finance committee before whom in review every item of expenditure may go, with the idea that it will be looked into closely and competently and thoroughly. On these two grounds I would like to urge on the first minister that he take also into consideration the absolute necessity of rescuing that committee from the intolerable and mainly useless position in which it has been placed during these many years past. It has not done the work it should have done; it never 'will under its present constitution, and it is too bad that you must take many hours out of hard worked members of parliament, and pit them against each other in that committee where from the very moment they enter the room until the session is wer they know there is very little chance of getting at the facts of any one case let alone a general revision of the public expenditure. You get rid of that unreasonable party spirit in the committee if you lessen the number of its members, and you will, I think, go largely towards effecting a great reform.
But another way of doing it is that the reasonable views of the first minister and the Minister of Finance as they have been expressed here to-day be impressed upon the members of the government who form that committee that the policy so reasonably laid down and fairly expressed this afternoon by both these gentlemen should be the policy which should rule in the Public Accounts Committee. Give some grace and favour to the opposition; ask yourselves one question and answer it. Ask: Would there be an item of the public expenditure in any year ever looked into if it remained for the members in that committee who represent the government to do so. The answer comes that it has not been done in the past and that it will probably not be done in the future. More than one half of the members of that committee are not doing their work and the other less than half are being hindered from doing it. Lessen the committee and at the same time let the reasonable attitude advanced this afternoon by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance imbue itj members and better work will be done. For myself I am a hard worked member of parliament; I came here to work and I have worked every year I have been here, but I have lost very many most valuable hours in that Public Accounts Committee and have seen very little good come from my efforts until for the last year or two I have cut it out and have largely devoted myself to other kinds of parliamentary . work. That ought not to be. It ought to be the ambition of every hard working rncmbpr of narliament, to nut his force into *ont or two of the committees of this House and do the same hard work there that he does in the House itself. I am hoping for a great deal to come from this proposition Mr. FOSTER.

PAPINEAU (Beauharnois) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 48) to amend the Railway Act. He said: The object of the Bill is to amend subsection 1 of section 298 of the Railway Act. This subsection was the subject of an amendment passed by parliament last session. It deals with the liability of a railway company for damage caused to property by fires started by a locomotive. It enacts first that in every case the railway company shall be liable for such damage. Then it declares that if it is shown that the railway company has used modern and efficient appliances, its liability shall be limited to $5,000 no matter what the value or the number of the properties injured or destroyed by the fire may be. The amendment of this
subsection passed last session provides that the railway company, though liable to the amount of $5,000 shall have the benefit of such insurance as the property owner of the property destroyed may have had on the property. The company shall be entitled to deduct from the amount of its liability the amount of such insurance. This deprives the property owner practically of his recourse against the railway company. If, for instance, a property of the value of $15,000 is destroyed, and it is insured for $5,000, the company has a right to deduct this amount, which leaves it with no damages to pay, and the owner loses the balance. Previous to the adoption of this amendment, the railway company would have been liable for $5,000, the owner would have recovered $5,000 of insurance, and would have lost $5,000. Now, instead of this, the $5,000 of insurance goes to the railway company and the property owner loses $10,000. For these reasons I think this amendment should be repealed. As there were three amendments of the same section made by the Act of 1909, I have thought it best by my Bill to repeal the whole section and draft a new section.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

1.	Eleven.

3.	Montreal.-Six cargo inspectors are employed at this port to watch the handling of perishable freight as it is unloaded from the cars and loaded into the steamships, to test the temperature of butter before it is placed in the cold storage chambers in the ships, to report the condition of the refrigerator chambers before loading is commenced and the ventilation of the holds in which perishable cargo is stowed and to place thermographs (self-recording thermometers) in refrigerator and cooled air chambers and in the holds in which perishable freight is carried. Particular attention is also paid to the deliveries of cheese and butter by river boats at Montreal.
Halifax.-During the winter months an inspector is employed at this port to look after the loading of apples and other perishable freight and to install thermographs in the fruit carrying steamers.
Ports in Great Britain.-Five cargo inspectors are employed to report the condition in which Canadian cheese, butter, eggs, fruit, &c., are landed from the steamers and the manner in which these products are handled while being unloaded and to advise the steamship officials of any rough handling and to report same to the department as well. They also retest the temperature of the specially marked packages of butter which have been tested by the Montreal inspectors, remove the thermograph records and send them promptly to Ottawa and interview importers on matters affecting the trade in farm and food products.
4.	Since the cargo inspection work was undertaken leading provision firms in Montreal, Liverpool, London and Glasgow have written the department expressing their appreciation of the beneficial results that have followed the appointment of inspectors at these ports.
During recent years the conditions under which Canadian produce is handled at the ports in Great Britain have been greatly improved. Previously there was considerable delay in the removal of shipments from the docks, but the inspectors have

succeeded in preventing this to a great extent and now as a rule Canadian shipments are handled with despatch.
The thermographs which are placed by the cargo inspectors in steamships at the ports of Montreal and Halifax have been a very important factor in improving the efficiency of the cold storage transportation, and have also been the means of bringing about more thorough systems of ventilation in the ordinary holds of the steamers.

In discussing this question it is hardly necessary that I should point out that it is of the utmost importance to the three maritime provinces. I have bracketed them together in connection with my resolution because they have all suffered in the same way, though not to the same extent, and they have suffered for the same reasons. Prince Edward Island more than the other two, because she has only the fisheries and agriculture as her natural resources, while Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have minerals, lumber, fisheries, and agriculture to depend upon; they are the eastern gateway of Canada and attract to their ports the trade of Canada, particularly the winter trade, and hence it is that they do not feel to the same extent perhaps as Prince Edward Island the decrease in their representation. In connection with this important subject I shall give the House some statistics which I hope may be found interesting. In 1867, when the four provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick agreed to form the Dominion of Canada, Ontario was allowed 82 members in the federal parliament, Nova Scotia 19, New Brunswick 15, and Quebec the unit of 65. In 1873 Prince Edward Island came into confederation under the census of 1871 and according to the census of that year the population of the provinces was as follows: Quebec, 1,191,516; Nova Scotia, 387,800; New Brunswick, 285,594; Ontario, 1,620.851; Prince Edward Island, 94,021.
The representation of Quebec being fixed at 65 members and the unit of representation being one-sixty-fifth of the population of Quebec, that unit under the census of 1871 was 18,331, which gave Nova Scotia an increase of two members making 21 members and 2,849 of a population over, it gave New Brunswick 15 units and 10,629 of a population over, which being over one-half the unit, allowed New Brunswick to have a representation of 16 members; it gave Ontario 88 units with 7,723 of a population ever or less than one-half the unit. These 88 members represented an increase of 6 members on the previous representation. It would have given Prince Edward Island 5 units with 2,366 or one-eighth of the unit of population over, but Prince Edward Island was given six representatives at that time. Later on I shall go into the question of why that was done. The decade between 1871 and 1881 saw a lar^e increase in the population of the maritime provinces and of Ontario. The times were prosperous down there and the population [DOT] increased largely so that according to the census of 1881, Quebec had a popula tion of 1.359,027, or a gain of 160,000; Nova Scotia had a population of 440,572, a gain of over 50,000, New Brunswick had a population of 321.233. a gain of 35,000; Ontarii had a population of 1,926,922, a gain of 21}
over 300,000, and Prince Edward Island had a population of 108.891, a gam of nearly 15,000. It will be seen that all of the provinces during that decade from 1871 to 1881 made substantial and respectable gains, notably the province of Ontario, notwithstanding that during that decade there was severe depression throughout Canada, Then in the census of 1881 the unit of representation Was increased to 20,908 or 2,500 more than in 1871, and this gave the four provinces other than Quebec the following representation in the House of Commons: Nova Scotia, 21 members, and 1,504 of a population over; New Brunswick, 15 members and 7,613 of a population over, which being less than half the unit New Brunswick lost one of her representatives; Ontario 92 members, with 3,386 of a population over, giving her an increase of four members on the previous parliament, and Prince Edward Island five members and 4,351 of a population over, which was only about one-fifth of the unit, and yet the island retained her six members. Again I ask why was that?
The decade between 1881 and 1891 showed a reduced increase in Quebec and practically no increase at all in the maritime provinces. It was a period of stagnation so far as the population of these provinces was concerned, and although there was a growth in Ontario and Quebec it was not. of very great extent. According to the census of 1891, Quebec had a population of 1,488,535; Nova Scotia 450,396, a gain of 10,000; New Brunswick 321,263, practically the same population as before; Ontario 2,114,321, and Prince Edward Island 109,078, or an infinitesimal gain. I shall, before I conclude, discuss what were the causes of this falling off, because I agree with the remark of the Finance Minister, addressed to the House a few days ago, that if you find that something happens you will likely see that there is a cause, and if you try you can discover what that cause is. I shall endeavour to present to the House some of the causes which led to this deplorable result. Now, the census of 1891 gave a unit of 22,900, or 2,000 more than the unit of 1881. The four provinces other than Quebec were under that census represented as follows:' Nova Scotia, 19 members, and 15,296 of a (population over, which toeing greater than half the unit allowed her 20 members^ or one less than she had on the previous census; New Brunswick had 14 members and 663 of a population over, giving her 14 representatives, or another loss of one member, and bringing her representation down to one less than when she *ntered confederation; Ontario got 92 members and 7,521 of a population over, leaving her representation the same as it was under he previous census; Prince Edward Island had 4 members and VM78 of a population

the trade and commerce, not only of Quebec itself, but of Ontario and the other' western provinces as well. It is the summer gate of commerce from the west and has to be improved. I do not know what the population of Montreal is at present, but I think it will be found at the next census to touch the half million mark. And I judge by the progress of the past few years, the time is not far distant when it will touch a million, and I hope that time will come soon. But in order to bring about the growth and expansion and consequent increase of population in the province of Quebec and particularly in the city of Montreal, this parliament had to spend, and rightly spend, enormous sums in order to create the channels and arteries by which trade and commerce would come. Already in imnroving the harbour of Montreal, some $12,000,000 have been spent, and it is in contemplation in the course of a few years to spend $18,000,000 more in order to make its harbour facilities equal to those of any port in the world. And it is perfectly right and proper that that should be done, but it means a lot of money. When we came into confederation in 1873, the St. Lawrence was a great river but you could not get ships drawing such draft of water up that river as now go up. You had to dredge it from end to end and make it so that large ships could get up in order that the trade and commerce, which naturally belongs to Canada, should find its way through this great Canadian port, and not through ports foreign to Canada. The consequence is we have spent enormously to dredge and improve that great waterway. You are going to make it practically a great canal. You have it down to something like 30 feet but that is not enough. The hon. Minister of Marine will have to undertake more work. Thirty feet is nothing extraordinary now. He will have to go on and deepen it to 40 feet, and that it should be done in the interests of Canada as a whole.
It is necessary, in order to bind the parts of Canada more closely together and to keep in our own channels the commerce which belongs to us. Therefore, so far as I am concerned, as one member of this House, although it is no particular advantage to me or my constituency, I recognize the need of that work and am just as strong in support of it as any gentleman living in Montreal itself. It is true this process of improving transportation develops other parts of the country than the province of Quebec, but I confine myself to a consideration of the effect upon Quebec because that is. the pivotal province. Enormous sums have been spent in other ways which must benefit the city of Montreal and Quebec generally. Consider the effect of one of our earliest works, the Intercolonial. That railway was built, of course, as a part of the compact of confederation, to induce the four Mr. WAKBTJRTON.
provinces to come together, it having been made, I believe, a sine qua non that this railway should be built to connect the maritime provinces with old Canada. It is true that this railway greatly benefits the maritime provinces. But it has been an enormous benefit also to the province of Quebec and the provinces further west. Long before other railways were in existence it afforded a means of carrying the manufactures of the west ro the maritime provinces, and the manufacturers of Canada generally admit that the markets of the maritime provinces are among the best they have. It still does that. Of course, this road was not built solely for the benefit of Quebec or of the other provinces. What I desire to point out is not so much what the object is as what the result has been. The effect of these improvements of which I have spoken is to greatly increase the opportunfties of employment in the great city of Montreal and so to increase greatly the population of that city and other parts of the province of Quebec. Montreal contains thousands and probably hundreds of thousands of people who but for these improvements in transportation would never have gone to help in building up the prosperity and the population of that great city. And now we have the great railways coming down from the west, the Canadian Pacific railway and the new Transcontinental. There is no question but that the Transcontinental will open up vast territories in the north of Quebec as well as Ontario and will gradually draw a large population to that region, with the result that the unit of representation will rise. Of course, we are all glad of these prospective additions to our population. I do not believe in a sectional view of these matters, for a benefit to one province is a benefit to the whole of Canada. Still, the result is that, through these enormous expenditures, expenditures made not only by the present government but by the several governments that preceded it, and made in pursuit of a well-defined and laudable policy carried out by all governments, which, though they may have differed in details and in questions of degree have always favoured the carrying out of this policy of development-population in the pivotal provinces has been increased and the unit of representation raised. Nor is the work finished, it goes on and will go on. There is the territory of Ungava, which is not now a part of the province of Quebec, but probably will be. This -will mean a further addition to the population of Quebec. It is true there are few people in Ungava now, but we know enough of the resources of Ungava to lead us to believe that many will be attracted to that territory, and, in speaking of this matter I think of the future as well as the present. This will further raise the unit

of representation, making our chances o regaining our lost representation very poo indeed. The further improvement of oui canals, and especially the enlargement o' the Welland and other canals, will add ti the result that we have already seen. So it is a rather forlorn prospect that is pre sented to us, with this great province pi Quebec growing by leaps and bounds witl' the result that our representation is going down. Even the regular public expend! ture is having the effect of promoting the opening up of the west and developing trade which ultimately benefits the city of Montreal. As you fill up the west you bring nearer the time when hundreds of millions of dollars worth of grain, besides other products of enormous value, will be annually produced for export, thus giving still more employment to the people of that province in which is our greatest port and which is the unit of representation, and so increasing the population of the province of Quebec. This great west, on the other, takes people from us. Many of those who were constituents of members from Prince Edward Island are now in the west. If the Prince Edward Island voters in that country were to throw their influence all on one side they would easily influence an election. I believe that in half of the constituencies west of the Great Lakes electors from Prince Edward Island hold the balance of electoral power. There are hundreds of teachers alone, now engaged in training the children of the west, who came from Prince Edward Island. All these, I am sure, have a warm spot in their hearts for their old sea-girt home. And if my words should reach them, as I hope they will reach some of them, I am sure that they will sympathize with me in desiring to see the representation of Prince Edward Island restored to that which she originally had.
The objection raised to the plea of Prince Edward Island in this matter is the old cry ' representation by population.' That is a most excellent general rule. But, like all general rules, it has its exceptions, and the exception proves the rule. When British Columbia entered confederation an exception was made. They drafted theii terms better than we did, inserting the word * increased ' when we said ' readjusted.' They came into the Union with six representatives in this House, and at that time, I think, they had scarcely white population enough to make up the number of the unit of representation. They have continued to grow. But what I point out is that the principle was recognized that special conditions should be recognized in this matter-the principle of representation by population was not carried out in its entirety. Nor do we carry it out with uniformity to-day. The unit of population is
25,000 odd, but take the case of the city of Montreal. I do not know what is the population of its several constituencies, but I think I am safe in saying that none of them is lower than 40,000, which would be 15,000 more than the unit. I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, but that your own constituency has a population a good deal greater than the unit. The same applies to the city of Toronto and other portions of Canada. The reason for these variations is that the local conditions are taken into consideration. It is obvious that when you deal with a city population, concentrated on a few square miles, those people can make their public wants felt much more readily than can a scattered population such as that of your constituency or mine. The question of remoteness also is taken into consideration, and I have no doubt that it was this element that caused the representatives of the Dominion government, away back in 1873, to concede to British Columbia a representation much greater than the application of the principle of representation by population would have given. The system of representation by population has been ignored in the United States in relation to the Senate. It was applied in the case of the House of representatives, but the framers of the Constitution, desiring to protect the smaller and weaker states, provided that each state should have the same representation in the Senate regardless of population. I do not know that the Senate of the United States has quite fulfilled the expectations of those who created it, but that is neither here nor there: the idea was to give each state equal representation in the Senate in order to protect the smaller.
It is not necessary for me to go at greater length into this question. I think that I have said enough to bring the matter fairly before the House; and I think the subject is of sufficient importance to justify me in so doing. I have not the acquaintance with the conditions prevailing in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick when they entered confederation that I have of those that prevailed and prevail in my own province. But I have no doubt that hon. members from those provinces who have the facts at their fingers' ends will be quite prepared to advance arguments in support of the restoration of their former representation. With these remarks, Mr. Speaker, and thanking the members of the House for their courtesy in listening to me on a subject which may appear to some of them trite, I beg to move the resolution standing in my name.
At six o'clock House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The motion to which my hon. friend

from Queens, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Warburton) has addressed himself this afternoon is, of course, one to which no objection can be taken. It is a very proper motion, and we will be happy to bring down any papers that may be in our possession in relation to the subject. I do not hesitate to say that personally I sympathize very warmly with my hon. friend in the good purpose he has in view; and if, by any stroke of my pen, I could restore to Prince Edward Island her lost representation, 1 can tell my hon. friend I should be exceedingly happy to do so. Possibly I see more clearly than he does the difficulties which arise in the way. I have no doubt that if, at the time the terms of union with Prince Edward Island were under consideration, any representatives of the Island had asked for a clause to be inserted to the effect that the representation of the Island should never be less than the numoer with which it started, I do not anticipate that anybody would have seriously oh-jected to such a provision. We have such a provision, not exactly in so many words, but there is a like provision in relation to British Columbia, and if it should so happen that by reason of that provision British Columbia should at any time have one or two members more than she would otherwise have, I do not think any of the other provinces would regard it as a very great grievance. And I have no doubt that if, at the proper time, somebody on behalf of Prince Edward Island had made the request, it is altogether probable that no serious objection would have been taken. Still we have to deal with the matter as it stands. The Confederation Act is a compact between various provinces; and even though we should feel, or the people of any one province should feel, that the terms of union were not working out as well as we might like, we have to recognize the fact that we cannot expect those terms to be, changed by any mere will of our own; we have to consider what would be the attitude of the other provinces as well. Now,. I think it would be a gracious thing if the great provinces of Quebec and Ontario, not to mention any of the others, should see the matter just as my hon. friend sees it, and say, * Yes, we will readily agree to such a change as would preserve the representation of Prince Edward Island, and perhaps of several other provinces as well '-that would, of course, be a very happy solution. But I have to return to the point I first made, that this is a matter of compact between the several provinces. We know our friends in the province of Ontario have always attached great importance to what they used to term rep. by pop.-representation by population; and it is well to understand the fact that if that principle had not been recognized the union could never Mr. FIELDING.
have been brought about. I fancy that the good people of Ontario may attach enough importance to that principle to-day to object to a change of the constitution, or to a departure from that principle, which would be involved in the proposition of my hon. friend. If, as a result of the discussion which my hon. friend gave the subject to-day, and of other discussions which he may perhaps congratulate himself on opening up, we should find that the change which he desires could be brought about by the good will of the other provinces, no one would be more pleased than myself. But I know the difficulties in the, way; therefore I should not encourage my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island to expect very quickly the result which he desires.
Motion agreed to.
