Mr. FISHER moved that the Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go

into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Manitoba Grain Act, chapter 83 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, as follows:-
By repealing subsection 5 of section 17, subsection 5 of section 47, and subsection 2 of section 109, and amending section 104, by substituting for the words ' license fee of two dollars' the words ' required license fee.'
By authorizing the Governor in Council to fix the respective fees to be paid for licenses under the Act, and by providing fines for contravention of the said Act.
Motion agreed to, and the House went into committee on the resolution.
What are these subsections that are repealed?

By substituting 'required license fee' for 'license fee of $2' it is proposed to change the system under which the fee is collected. At the present time all elevators have to pay the same license fee of $2, but there is a decided difference in the amount of business done in different elevators, and, therefore, they wish to measure the license bv the amount of business done. The words have'to be changed in the Act to 'required license fee.'
That seems to have reference to amending section 109, but the minister has not told us what he proposes to repeal.
These words occur in different places in the Act, and the sections mentioned in the resolution are the sections in which they occur; therefore, they all require to be amended.
What is the idea of the minister as to the fee that should be exacted?

I could not give an exact statement as to the amount, but it will vary according to the business done in the different elevators. Some of the large elevators will have to pay more than $2. I do not think it is intended that any elevator shall have its license for less than $2.
At the present time the Governor in Council may impose fines. Have you any knowledge of the fines that are contemplated in the Act? This appears to be a new authority.

That section changes the form of the proceedings. At present the proceedings under the Act are in the form of an indictment, whereas, it is desired that these proceedings be taken under the Summary Convictions Act. and that changes in the Act are required for that purpose. I have no memorandum from the Department of Trade and Commerce as to how
great the fines may be. These fines are imposed by regulation.
Were they heretofore imposed by the statute itself? Does it propose to change that now and give power to the Governor in Council to impose fines by regulation?
It means that you are providing for fines by the Bill?

Yes, I have the Bill here:
Any person required by this section to furnish such statement or declaration, and failing to do so within three days after receipt of a written demand to him therefor from the commissioner, shall be liable upon summary conviction, to a fine of twenty-five dollars for each day thereafter during which he shall fail to furnish such statement or declaration, and the minister shall have power to cancel his license.
Licenses issued under this Act shall be revocable by the commissioner upon a summary proceeding before the commissioner upon complaint of any person, in writing, under oath setting forth the particular violation of the law, and upon satisfactory proof in that behalf to be taken in such manner as is directed by the commissioner; provided that such revocation shall not take effect until the minister has given his sanction thereto.
I do not see anything defining any other exact amount, and I do not find anything in the Bill prescribing any other fines than the sections which I have just read. I think that must be the one that is referred to in the resolution.

I would like to ask the minister on what representation he is making these amendments. Has there been a petition presented, or has a delegation waited upon the minister to point out defects in the Act, or where the Act could be strengthened in any way? This is the first intimation I have had that the Act was going to be amended.

As far as 1 know these amendments originated in the department to facilitate the working of the Act. I am not aware that they have not been asked for but I have no officer of the department with me to-night and I could not positively answer that question. Of course, this is merely the resolution upon which the Bill is founded.

There certainly must have beeh some communication from the officials representing the government of Manitoba or this amendment would not be advanced by the minister. I would like to know what representations have been made.

I have no information about any representations. If the hon. gentleman considers it necessary, before proceeding with the Bill itself, to have that information I would have to ask the committee to rise and report progress.

I think it would be well to have all the information which we can have before any such amendment takes place. I rather agree with the minister that it would be well to ask the committee to rise and report progress and let us get some further information.
All the information will be available when the Bill itself comes up for consideration. I think it would be well perhaps to let the resolution go through.

I have no objection providing this resolution does not commit us , to any particular amendment. I fancy that if this resolution is allowed to pass the argument will be put forward, as it has been put forward on other occasions, that we have committed ourselves to the amendment. I do not know that we will retard the business of the House very much if we ask the minister to have printed, or laid on the table of the House, such information as he has with respect to the request for these particular amendments.

The Bill is printed, but it cannot be distributed until it is introduced. The Bill will not be introduced until the resolution is adopted. I am just waiting for the adoption of the resolution to introduce the Bill. The Bill will be distributed the moment it is introduced. The information my hon. friend asks for will certainly be available when the Bill comes up for discussion, and it is quite open to the House to reject any portion of the Bill or amend it; so that the passing of the resolution does not in any way prevent the discussion, amendment, or rejection of any particular clause in the Bill.

I think it would be well to pass this resolution. I may say to the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples), that there has been some request for some amendments from the representative of the farmers, the man who looks after any difficulties that the farmers have.
Who is that?

Mr. D. D. Campbell, of Winnipeg. He has represented that some amendments are necessary to carry out the evident intention of the Bill of last year. I took these amendments up with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and he is of the opinion they are reasonable amendments, and although they do not appear in the Bill as introduced they will be passed later on. The sooner they are passed the better. The amendment to which I particularly refer is in connection with broken and small wheat. At present the elevators are not compelled to account for the screenings of wheat and this year in some cases there have been 100 bushels of screenings, which make first-class feed, cleaned out of a 1,000 bushel car. The farmer has to pay Mr. FISHER.	/
the freight on the screenings but at present the elevators can, if they wish, retain them. An amendment is to be introduced in this Bill to make it compulsory on the inspector to state, when he inspects a car, what percentage of dockage there shall be for number one or number two screenings, and the elevator in addition to giving a certificate of the out-turn of the whole wheat must also give a certificate of the out-turn of the screenings provided the screenings amount to over two per cent. Number one screenings will be the screenings that have over 50 per cent of wheat broken, and number two screenings under 50 per cent.
How could the inspector tell how much broken wheat there would be in any car and how could he distinguish one car from the other after passing through the elevator?
The inspector does that at present,
No.

He does, and the western members can tell my hon. friend that he does. The inspector at present says that it will take two per cent or five per cent or ten per cent to clean that car and that much is docked, but under the present system he does not say what that is, and the amendment will give the inspector the power to say what it will take to clean that car, and a separate certificate must be given the farmer for that if it is over two per cent. The inspector will also say whether it is number one or number two screenings. This year there has been as much as $40 or $50 worth of good feed taken out of a car which the elevator does not need to account for and the amendment is proposed to remedy that injustice.
Is that the intention of the Bill now introduced?
The Bill was drafted before I took the matter up with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but he agreed with me that these were necessary amendments and that he would have them passed.
What I want to know is on what advice the minister is amending the Act on the lines suggested in the resolution.

As I understand it from a short conversation with the Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce these amendments which are in the Bill have been found necessary to facilitate the working of the Act. I am not aware that any of the provisions in the printed Bill now ready are based on representations from any particular body. I am speaking subject to correction; the department may have had representations in regard to these in addition to their own experience in the working of the Act.

I know from personal experience that the farmers have suffered to a large degree because of the defects in the present system which the hon. member (Mr. Turriff) has referred to. I hope when the Bill comes down that it will have a provision for preventing the great loss of money which the farmers have suffered in this way in the past. There never was in the western crop, especially in Saskatchewan and Alberta, as large a percentage of broken grain as this year; a fact which is no doubt due to the well developed kernel . and the extremely dry weather during harvest. I believe it is necessary to have the amendments referred to passed as soon as possible, and I have therefore no objection to the resolution.

My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) and Macdonald (Mr. Staples) are both farmers and their interest is for the farmers, but the elevator men and the grain merchants are also interested in the grain business, and, and I think an opportunity should be afforded to them to express their views before the Bill is passed.

The amendment spoken of by my hon. friend from Assinboia (Mr. Turriff) is not contained in the Bill as printed. Probably the hon. gentleman himself will move it in the House at the proper stage of this Bill and it will be considered on its merits. I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) that if I have charge of the Bill at that stage I shall be only too happy to secure an opportunity for all the different interests being represented and heard.
Resolution reported, read the second time and agreed to.	[DOT]

House in Committee of Supply.
Arthabaska public building, $15,000.

A site has been purchased out of an appropriation made two sessions ago, and we are asking for this vote in order to proceed with the construction of the building.
Aylmer post office-addition to building, &c., $5,000.

This is tor the purpose of making necessary additions and improvements to the public building at Aylmer, a building which is now entirely out of repair.
Chicoutimi public building-ground improvements, $1,500.
This is for laying concrete sidewalks and macadam roadways around the public building.
What other public works are in progress at Chicoutimi?

There is dredging and, I think, a wharf.
Dominion public buildings Quebec-renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $20,000.
What was the amount spent at Sherbrooke last year?
What will be the amount this year?

I am not able to tell my hon. friend.
Fraserville armoury, $5,000.
This is to make provision for the nurchase of a site and the erection of an armoury, which has been requested by the Militia Department since October, 1907.
What regiment uses this?
The 89th Temiscouata and Rimouski regiment.
What will be the full cost of this building?
As near as I can tell, about $10,000.
Has it been arranged to put a shooting gallery in this building?
I am not able to say positively.

It would be a great source of benefit to the regiment and would not cost anything, because the basement could be utilized for the purpose.
Grasse Isle quarantine station-improvements and repairs to buildings, and fittings, furniture, &c., $7,000.

This is to make provision for the construction of new buildings and also repairs to the old buildings. These have all been asked for by "Dr. Martineau, the medical superintendent of the station.
Joliette armoury, $12,000.
This amount is asked to complete the erection of the building, which is now under contract.
Can the minister tell us numerically the strength of the force at Joliette?
It is the headquarters of the 83rd Joliette regiment and also a 1 company.
What will be the total cost?
Including everything, about $23,200.
Was there a drill shed there formerly, or what, accommodation had the regiment up to this time?
I really do not know as to that.
How many companies are accommodated there?
I think two.
Is the contract let?

Yes, and the building is very nearly finished. Six tenders were received. The lowest was accepted, $13,500. In addition there is heating, electric wiring and fittings, furniture, inside walks, fencing, contingencies and cost of site. The electric wiring and heating were, I think, let by tender, but I am not sure.
What did they cost?
The electric wiring, $512; heating and boilers together, $2,000. The building is two stories of brick, with stone foundation and trimmings; 56 feet 2 inches by 47 feet 1 inch.

According to the Militia list, there is only one company there. What is the hon. gentleman's policy with regard to armouries in general? Are any more being built? Why is it this one cost $23,000 and the one at Fraserville only $10,000, and how is it these are not paid out of the general vote for armouries of $50,000?

We are endeavouring to build one at Fraserville at less cost than at Joliette. _ Fraserville is the last. There is a strong disposition on the part of hon. members on both sides to try if possible to reduce the cost of armouries, and we have felt that in the case of Fraserville, we should get a suitable one for $10,000. In the case of Hartland, we are providing for a building at $10,000 which will also accommodate the post office.
-Mr. SAM. HUGHES. What regiment is that to accommodate?
Two companies of the 67th.
What is the size of the armoury at Fraserville?
The plans have not been prepared yet.

The headquarters of the 67th are at Woodstock, and we have already constructed an armoury there to accommodate a regiment of infantry and a battery of artillery. Why then erect an armoury at Hartland?

In the Woodstock armoury there are the 10th Field Battery, the First Company of the Engineers and two companies of the 67th. The remaining six companies of the 67th are at local headquarters. Two of them are at Hartland.
Is it the policy then, in addition to building armouries at headquarters for the regiments, to build armouries at other places for various companies?

The armoury at Hartland is not in pursuance of any general policy, but it was represented to us that the people would be well satisfied if we put up a building costing $10,000 which would do for a post office and might be used also for regimental purposes. That was done to meet the necessities of a particular case.

It would be more advisable to follow some uniform system. That has been discussed again and again in the House. There are a.great many regiments in this Dominion which have no armoury and which, so far as qualifications and service records go, are unsurpassed. I must certainly protest against the system pursued here. We understood that there was one bulk vote brought each year that is to be used for these armouries.

While there has been a vote taken of $50,000 each session for the construction of armouries in smaller towns, I do not think that that vote has been granted to the exclusion altogether of special votes for buildings which could not be erected out of the $50,000 vote. When I became minister, I found there was some departure from that rule, and that has been continued.
Why is Fraserville specially selected and Joliette and Hartland and other important places left out? Is there any reason for it?
Nothing more than I have given.
On what principle is that $50,000 apportioned?

This apportionment is made on the recommendation of the Militia Department. Last session, when I asked for the general vote, I gave a statement of how the money voted for the previous year had been expended. And when we come to that item I will give a statement for the expenditure on armouries for the past year.
Was there a post office building at Hartland before?
No.
On what principle would the selection be made of places in which the money is to be spent?

The Militia Department makes a requisition on the Public Works Department for the erection of certain armouries out of the general vote. We recognize that their judgment is to be relied upon and we proceed with the work, drawing on the vote for that purpose.
It would be the right of the Minister of Militia, of course, under the circumstances to recommend where an armoury was to be built, regardless of the judgment of parliament.
That is the object of getting the vote in that way.
Very convenient for the minister when an election is coming on.
That might be said, but I do not think that that has ever influenced the distribution.

I do not know whether this general vote has been long in existence or not. But, from the knowledge we have of this government, I should not have the highest expectation of such a vote would be distributed strictly on sound principles.

At this point I should explain to the committee, that while in the printed estimates there are two items connected with Grosse Isle station, I have called only one, as the resolution in my hand does not completely give the other. The second is:
Grosse Isle quarantine station-new detention building, $20,000.
I have entered it in the resolution. Does it carry?
This building is asked for by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher)-who tells me that there is absolute need of it.
How many immigrants will it house?
I have not that information before me, but no doubt the Minister of Agriculture will be glad to give the information.

This building is intended to take the place of the present second-class detention building. These detention buildings at Grosse Isle are to receive those who arrive in ships and who, though not themselves diseased, may have come in contact with disease on the ship and possibly bear the germs of that disease with them. We have there what is called a first-class detention building where the first-class passengers are accommodated. It offers about as good accommodation as the second-class on a steamship. In the present second-class detention building the accommodation is not better than the present steerage on board the vessels, and has been frequently
occupied by steerage passengers because we have not sufficient accommodation for all when a large number are to be detained. The new building will be about the grade of the first-class detention building at present, because the accommodation for second-class passengers aboard the ships is so much better than the present second-class detention building can offer. The new building will accommodate about 150 without crowding, with a possibility of putting into it 200 if necessary.
It affords sleeping accommodation, of course?

Much like the state-rooms on a steamer. The building has a passage down the middle with rooms about the size of state-rooms on a vessel on either side. There are two stories of these. In the centre of the building are the dining and sitting rooms. There are wings on either side with the rows of state-rooms.
And bath-rooms, &c.?

Yes, about the same accommodation as is afforded on the river steam-boats on the St. Lawrence. There is a bath-room at either end. As a rule, the ladv passengers are housed at one end of the building and the gentlemen at the other, with exceptions in the case of married people.

I would like very much to give my hon. friend a definite assurance in regard to the cost of this building, including the site, but I am not able to do so for the reason that I do not know what it will cost us to procure a suitable site in the first place. I am not able to state to the committee to-night what we will get a suitable site for, and I am not able to tell the committee positively what the building will cost, but my own impression is that we ought to get a building at Maisonneuve which would not cost us over $30,000 or $35,000. That would be exclusive of the site. Of course, in a city like Montreal, which is growing very rapidly, we must be prepared to pay something more for a public building than we would in one of the smaller towns.
Mr! HENDERSON. I am afraid the minister has taken a very wide range. Thirty thousand or $35,000 would put up a pretty handsome building, but I think that between his maximum and his minimum there is too wide a difference. I think he should be able to say to the committee that he considers $30,000 ample. If he does not think so let him tell the committee that he will instruct his officers not to go beyond the larger sum. Let him fix some definite sum, because, if he does not do so, he can rest assured that the amount, no matter what it is, will be very greatly exceeded. The minister says that he does not know what the site will cost. I am not asking him to declare how much he will expend on this building, including the site. We will leave tne site in abeyance. That mav cost $1,000, it mav cost more, it may cost less; but let the minister tell us now just how much he is going to sav to his officers that the building will cost exclusive of the site. There is no difficulty in doing that. The minister knows how much money he can afford to

spend on a building of that kind. It is not a question of whether it shall be $30,000 or $35,000. The minister is going to erect a building and he says: The country can afford to spend $30,000 or $35,000. That is the only way in which the minister, or the House, can keep a check upon the expenditure of the country, and I do say that before this vote is passed the minister must definitely give us the assurance that the amount to be expended shall not exceed a certain sum, and let him name that sum exclusive of the site if he thinks fit.

As this proposed building is in my constituency, I may be permitted to say a word upon it. An amount has been mentioned as the probable value of land in Maisonneuve, but I should like to point out that you cannot buy land there as cheaply as some hon. members may imagine. You cannot buy a site for a postal station for much less than between $8,000 and $10,000. If a postal station is to be built there it will not be to please people in Maisonneuve but to satisfy the requirements of the postal department. Under these circumstances I think the minister rather underestimates when he mentions $35,000 as being the amount which will be required to satisfy the postal requirements 'of that community which is growing very fast. In the near future it will be absolutely necessary to have a building large enough to provide for tlfe growing business of the postal department in that section. Is it annexed?

It is not annexed yet, but will be next year. They are annexing everything around the city of Montreal just now and it will be brought in next year. My hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) rather surprised me when he stated that the site for a public building in this town would cost as much as $10,000. He may be right. I have no knowledge of the value of land there. But, I made a fair proposition to the minister. We leave out of consideration the site and only ask the minister as to the amount which will be expended upon the building. I have a little suspicion about the cpst of Mr. HENDERSON.
this building. No doubt when he comes to erect it the workmen will have to work only eight hours a day. The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) has an eight hour a day Bill before the House.

The hon. member from Maisonneuve may have something to say upon that. He is supporting the government and he will expect the government to support him. What about the hon. gentleman's Bill providing for an eight hour day on public works. It would be a most remarkable thing after the hon. gentleman's advocacy of an eight hour day for public works that he should permit a public building to be erected in his riding and the men be called'upon to work ten hours. Surely the hon. gentleman would not permit it. He would not want public money expended in his county if the men had to work ten hours a day. So that we can take it for granted that it would be an eight hour a day job, and of course it will cost a great deal more than if it were a ten hour a day job, because the men will reasonably expect to get as much for eight hours as they would get for ten. The figure I named was exclusive of the site.

I am not very much concerned as to what the cost of the building will be. I do not know anything about the size of the town or the requirements of the place, but I want to establish the principle so that we will know just exactly what we are doing. Now we understand the minister that whatever the site costs is 'not to be a portion of this $35,000, but that the building, outside of the site, is not to cost more than $35,000 when completed, lighted, the walks around it, the grass planted and everything done that will make it a place of beauty so that the government will not be called upon to expend another dollar upon it.
Did I give that assurance?

I want the minister to give us that assurance. If we allow the latitude that has prevailed in the past the

expenditure is bound to get beyond our control. Has the minister the plans and specifications before him?
No.

Then perhaps it is so much the better because he can direct his architect to produce a building which will not cost more than $35,000, and if the architect does not do it he should get another architect. But I am perfectly confident the architect will and can do it if he is so instructed.
If it does cost more than $35,000 the hon. gentleman will want to know the reason why.

Oh, the hon. gentleman can easily find a reason or an excuse; he could give the eight hour day movement as a reason, but here we are spending the money of the people and the minister should not treat it as a joke. I have advocated this in the House for many a year, and one Minister of Public Works told me that my plan was a good one and that when we were voting away the money of the country we should know just how much we were voting.

I enter my protest against the utterly reckless manner in which the money of the country is being handled by this government. I do not think that even this House has ever seen such an exhibition as the Minister of Public Works has afforded in respect to this item. A year ago he asked for' $10,000 to erect a building in Maisonneuve, and one would naturally suppose that was all that was needed, but this year he asks for $20,000, and before we have had time to realize it, he tells us the building wall cost $30,000 or $35,000. Then the member for the constituency tells us that the land alone will cost $8,000 or $10,000 and the Minister of Public Works immediately tries to excuse himself for his intention to pile on something like $15,000 or $20,000 more than he is asking for to-night. Surely the minister should know what a building will cost before he asks for money for it, but he has no more idea of the ultimate cost of this building than a child on the street. That is our, experience of him in connection with other buildings. The cottages for the servants of the Military College at Kingston were contracted for at $77,000, and then he asked for $112,000, and after spending two weeks trying to justify himself he finally agreed to knock off $20,000 from the vote. Last year his excuse for the large amount of money these cottages cost was that the foundations had to be dug out of the solid rock, but as a matter of fact there were not over three feet of rock excavated. The wall above the ground is over four feet high and allowing eight feet for the cellar, 1 22
I do not see how he can make out that the excavation is as much as he said. But that is the way the money goes; drill halls here and there for the accommodation of the soldiers and the soldiers to-day at Kingston are out on Barriefield. common providing films for a moving picture show. I protest against the minister asking an appropriation for a building until he is able, to tell us what that building will ultimately cost.

Maisonneuve is a very important centre, and I am satisfied the minister will not erect a suitable building there for $25,000, but I want to ask him if he is providing that the public buildings erected by the government shall have 100 feet, or even 200 feet, of space all round them so as to separate them from adjoining buildings? That is the practice in the United States and a very good practice it is.
If we made any such rule as that it would cost us a great deal of money.
Even so.
I admit it might be in the public interest to do so.
It would.
We have not adopted that rule and we are not going to do so in this case.

In the country towns you will find some of these buildings erected between a corner grocery and a saloon, when it would be just as easy for the government to acquire a suitable site. I would suggest to the member for Maisonneuve that he should select a proner site and even if it cost a few thousand dollars extra the House will not begrudge it.

Surely the minister must know what the ultimate cost of this building will be, and the House certainly has the right to know, before we are asked to vote this money. I would suggest that the minister let this item stand, as well as other items which may follow, until he is able to state to the House how much in each case shall be spent for a site and how much for a building to be erected thereon. I for one do not feel justified in letting an item of this kind go through without a proper statement from the minister.

I thought I stated very frankly to the committee what was the situation in regard to this building. Maisonneuve is a part of the city of Montreal; it is growing very rapidly, and land there has a value which is based upon that growth. The hon. member who represents the constituency states that in his judg-i ment the site will cost between $8,000 and



$10,000. In my opinion the building will cost not less than between $30,000 and $35,000. I shall ask the chief architect to plan a building that will cost about that amount, though if a suitable building would cost $5,000 or even $10,000 more, I think we should still proceed with it. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) complains that while I am asking fo-r $20,000, I intimate that the building is going to cost more. When my hon. friend has more parliamentary experience, he will know that the total amount required for the construction of any public work is never asked for in the first vote unless it is expected that the work will be completed during the year. All that is asked is the amount expected to be spent in the year.
Is it also the case that when a minister asks for an appropriation for a public building, he gives no estimate of the cost of that building?

That is the point I am making now.

A postal station.

It is a post office at present, because Maisonneuve is outside the city of Montreal. When it is joined to Montreal, this will he a postal station.

I understand that the Postmaster General contemplates having a postal station there, and that is what it ought to be called. Did I understand the minister to say that he had not yet any plans prepared for this building?
Not yet.

It does seem to me to he a little peculiar in the minister to ask for a vote of $20,000 without a plan. "When he comes and asks for an appropriation for a public building, he ought to be able to lay the plans on the table of the House. What are we giving the vote for? Not on the strength of the minister's assertion. We are going on a plan and a plan which is tangible and can be got at; and when we are asked for $30,000, we want to know the plan of the building. The minister says he has not got any. It turns then entirely on the minister's assertion, so that it is perfectly proper that he should have his land before he asks us for the vote. Thei minister might very well take a vote and purchase the land, but until he submits his plan for the building, it seems to me not proper for him to ask the House for a vote for the building and then give no definite promises because he has no plans on which to base them.

If my hon. friend will assure the committee that during the time he was in charge of the finances of the country, he ever knew of an instance when plans were laid on the table with reference to public buildings for which votes were passed, there would be some force in his argument.

My hon. friend is always at his old trick of going back to the past. Might I retort by asking, if during the time when he was a Liberal-Conservative and supported that party, and at other times he was half' way between the two parties, on the fence, as an independent, and at others when he dropped down on the other side of the fence as soon as he felt the attractions of patronage, I suppose that kind of reminiscence would rather bother him and he would not consider it was the best way of conducting business. But suppose we consider that he is responsible for the votes he asks us to pass when he brings down the estimates, are we not justified in asking him to submit the plans for the buildings he asks us to authorize him to construct.

If the hon. gentleman chooses to go back to the days when he used to live away down by the sea, before he found it necessary to change his political residence and move westward to Toronto, and if he would call to mind the thousands of dollars squandered, so far as New Brunswick was concerned, by his own neglect of the interests of people in the city of St. John, by his refusal to recognize their legitimate aspirations to have that port become the winter port of Canada, and his recognition apparently that it was quite proper to vote subsidies out of the people's money for Atlantic steamers which passed by the port of the city of St. John and made their terminus at a foreign port, assisted by the moneys of Canada, despite the pleadings of the people for some recognition of their rights, he would probably have no difficulty in discovering why so many of the best people there changed their politics and supported a party which is disposed to do justice to the maritime provinces. Now as to why I have not brought down plans here to-night, I would say that in these estimates we have some twelve hundred items and that it would be out of the question for me to instruct my chief architect and chief engineer to prepare the plans before the items were submitted to the House and voted. Does he suggest that I should have had the plans prepared before my colleagues had agreed to the estimates and before they had been submitted for the consideration of the House? These estimates were only prepared and approved by council a few weeks ago, and it would he utterly impossible to prepare one-tenth of the plans of

the various public buildings and wharfs for the consideration of the committee at present. Were I to attempt to do so, it would be utterly impossible to go on with the consideration of these public works within any reasonable time. What I have said is that such and such a building is to cost a certain amount of money; and when the amount is voted, I shall ask the chief architect to prepare the plans in each case accordingly. In the particular case under consideration, I have said that the building, in my judgment, ought not to cost over $35,000, and I shall instruct the chief architect to prepare plans of a building which will not cost more than that sum.

Before the minister will instruct the chief architect to have the plans prepared would it not be advisable for him to have his site? Should he not first secure a site at Maisonneuve which would be of sufficient size to leave considerable space between the public building and any other adjoining building?

As soon as I can get the site, I shall have the plans prepared for a suitable building. I cannot get the site without getting the money appropriated. I am only asking for $20,000. If the site should cost $10,000, that will only leave $10,000 for the building.

Mr, FOSTER. Does the hon. minister not think it would be better to take a vote for the purchase of the site and have his plans prepared and ready at the next session so that the House will know what kind of building will be constructed? *

I venture to raise my voice in protest against this vote. I notice that one or two members bn the other side laugh. I wonder now, if they would conduct their own business in this way.

If the hon. member (Mr. Foster) will pardon me, there is one bit of further information which I wish to give.
I stated the population of Marieville at 1,306. I should have added that there is also the population of Ste. Marie de Man-noir who use the same post office, that population being 1,054, so that there is a total population of 2,360 to be accommodated by this post office.
Is that a town?
A village, I believe.
Does the minister know?
I am informed that Ste. Marie de Mannoir is a parish.

Ah! There is quite a difference, is not there? Marieville being in the parish, a post office built in Marieville will be in the parish, no doubt about that But there is equally little doubt that the $25,000 is spent for Marieville and not for the parish. Is there no post office in the parish outside of Marieville?
My information is that the parish of Ste. Marie de Monnoir will also use the post office.

There is no request from the Postmaster General, and no approval by him of this expenditure of $25,000. The Board of Trade have asked for it, we are told. This is not the money of the Board of Trade, this is the money of the country, and if it is spent at all it should be spent for no other purpose than to meet the postal requirements. Will the minister say that he has the approval and request of the Postmaster General for this vote, that he cannot carry on the postal business of this country in a proper way unless he gets $25,000 for a budding in Marieville? I have too much respect for the Postmaster General to believe that he would stand up in this House and make any such statement. The truth is that this is a matter of mere patronage, this $25,000 which has been raised from the taxation of the people is simply a matter of patronage at Marieville, nothing more, and nothing less. I for one am going to voice my protest against Marie-, ville having such an expenditure until I get good reasons from the Postmaster General to the effect that this expenditure of $25,000 is necessary in order to properly carry on the post office business of the country. I think we ought to make a very vigorous protest against any expenditure of that kind. The minister says in his bland way: Well, we think. Who are we?

The ministry. We think that a village of 1,300 people ought to have $25,000 spent on a post office. If the government thinks that, are you going to carry out the principle to its logical conclusion, and are you going to plant $25,000 of the people's money in every place in this country which has a population of 1,300? What is the post office revenue there?
From the post office, $1,396.59 ; from customs, $4,061.56.
What is the cost of the administration of the post office?

The postmaster's salary is $643. The money orders, savings bank and postal notes afford a revenue of $774.25. This building is to be used for customs purposes also, and the customs revenue must also be included with the post office revenue.

I fancy the Minister of Customs will not say to this House that he wants $25,000 spent in Marieville in order to enable him to carry on the customs business of the country. So it is not germane at all to say that customs must be added in. Now you have a surplus on that transaction of about $500 or $600. Put your $25,000 building there, and what will be the standing and permanent charge upon the country? It is absolutely wrong and the minister knows it, and I think he would be well advised if he allowed this item to stand until he hears from the Postmaster General, and until this committee get sufficient reasons from the men who are conducting te business.

Notwithstanding the judgment of the hon. gentleman, I do intend to endeavour to pass the vote-unless the committee should determine against it. But why does my hon. friend make such a dead set-if I may use the expression- against this item? He allowed the item of a public building at Hillsborough, which is a no larger place than Marieville, to go through without opposition. He made no protest against the vote for the erection of a public building in Athabaska, which I think is no more important than Marieville. Is it because the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was elected in that constituency by acclamation, that my hon. friend makes such determined opposition to this item? I do not think he knows the importance of this town, or he would not make such a determined opposition. I gave the population of Marieville of 1901, when it was 1,306. In the parish of Ste. Marie de Monnoir at the same time the population was 1,054. My information is that both the parish and the village use the post office in Marieville. Now the building is required for both post office and customs purposes, and the revenue which the country receives from these two sources was-upwards of $5,400 during the year 1908-9. Evidently a large business is being done there. The money orders issued amounted to $18,000, and the money orders paid to $14,000. My information is that Marieville-is a progressive town, new industries are constantly springing up. There are two hat factories carrying on successfully a manufacturing business. While the population in 1901 was 1,306, it has been growing steadily, and according to a census taken in 1907 it showed a population of 1,671. That would be in addition to the population of Ste. Marie de Monnoir. Now Marieville contains in addition to the factories I have mentioned, a college, a Roman Catholic -church, a Baptist church, an asylum for the aged and poor, a chamber of commerce, eleven stores, four hotels, one sawmill, a foundry, a threshing machine factory, a branch bank, and the ordinary express- and telegraph offices. So it is a place of importance, and increasing in population, and I certainly do think that my hon. friend had better look around and find some other public building against which he can direct his opposition with better ground. So far as I know, this place has no public building, and we are simply giving to the people what they are fairly entitled to.

Does not my hon. friend think that he might just as well have left out one portion of his remarks when_ he asked the question, by way of insinuation, if I opposed this vote simply because a minister of the Crown happened to have been elected there?'
You let so many others go through.

Does my hon. friend think that is a manly argument between a member and a minister? Does he really think so? I dare say he does or else he would not have used it. If he thinks so, I think very few people in this House will think so. Had he so poor a case that he had to appeal to his imagination and to a prejudiced imagination? Is that the kind of tactics my hon. friend has to use generally? Is his success due to that? He exemplifies it in this argument. I think my hon. friend would be better advised to leave insinuations like that out when we are discussing an important business matter >f this kind. 1 have no doubt there will be a great many others that I might protest against just the same as this one here. Vhen he attempts to put in places like Lhis $25,000 of the people's money, where -re we to end? I would like to have the 'ostmaster General's frank opinion in re-erence to this. I have found him a straight
*d honourable man and I would like to know whether he needs this. If he does

not that settles the question. I am looking into the eyes of people away out in the far distant districts that need things that they have not got, and why should we plant down $25,000 in these little places that are very well served now and leave the great development and progress of the country entirely unprovided for in so far as these extravagances in expenditure make it impossible to carry out these improvements? Are we not business men enough to look at it from a business point of view? Do we need to resort to petty insinuations to patch up a very bad case?
Will the minister give us the number of towns in the province which have not yet been favoured with post offices or public buildings whose population is greater than that of Marieville?
I could not give that.
What is the county seat of Rouville?
Marieville.

I took occasion last year, when matters of this kind were up, to point out that post offices were being built under the Public Works Department where they were absolutely unnecessary. I went into this question, looked up the history of fifty post offices, and I found that the cost averaged about $30,000. Suppose we place the interest on that at $1,200 and the cost of maintenance and repairs at $1,200; that makes $2,400 annually for keeping up these little post offices per annum. I found that prior to the new offices being built the government were paying less than $150	per annum each. The
business interests of this country would be better served by the government in these small places renting buildings for post offices purposes. They would save a large sum of money annually even if they were to raise the rental. There is no doubt that there are many men in Marie, ville and other small places who would be very glad to rent their premises to the government for, say, $200 a year and give the service that the public required. While we have large towns that have no public buildings and have no attention paid to their needs with respect to post office facilities, I think it is wrong to be spending public money in these small places. We have towns in the country having 7,000 population and whose gross postal income amounts to $10,000 that have no public buildings in which to conduct the post office business. They cannot secure buildings from the government which is ready to expend hundreds of thousands of dollars in villages where they are not required at all. In my riding we have three towns with a gross revenue in each one of them running from $5,500 to Mr. FOSTER.
$7,000 and yet they cannot get a post office. They are not considered large or important enough to warrant the government in the expenditure of public money upon the erection of a post office, but in other sections of the country, in little villages with a gross revenue of $1,300, buildings are erected because they are able to successfully besiege the minister and get money appropriated for that purpose. There seems to be a lack of any business plan or system to guide the Minister of Public Works in the distribution of public money. Every minister who is at the head of a department should make his application to the Minister of Public Works before he undertakes to erect a public building. The Minister of Militia should father the expenditure for the armouries that are erected under his department. The Postmaster General ought to make the recommendation and father the responsibility for the erection of a post office and the same should apply with regard to all the other departments that are under the charge of the government. It is utterly impossible for a Minister of Public Works-I do not care how well qualified he may be-to have that varied knowledge with regard to all the departments of the government which would warrant him in' coming to a conclusion upon every application placed before him. He ought to throw that responsibility on the heads of the department and then he should confine himself to carrying out the instructions that they give him and curtail his expenditure in proportion to the needs of the public. When the minister states that there is a population of 2,300 in these two villages that are supposed to be served by this post office and when he states that the total revenue is something over $1,300 he makes a most remarkable statement indeed. Any of the towns in my riding with a population of 2,300 would have a gross revenue of over $5,000 and I think there is something radically wrong with the statement of the minister when he says there is only a revenue of $1,300 from a population of 2,300. There is evidently not that number of people or they do not use the post office and if they do not use the post office I do not think we are justified in spending $25,000 in erecting a building of that size.

I want to call the attention of the committee, whether it be any use or not, to two other points. In a young country like Canada with a very large area and sparse population greatly scattered, the need for postal accommodation in the way of the carrying of letters and papers fortnightly, weekly, tri-weekly and daily is very great, and from all over that immense territory we have prayer after prayer, petition after petition asking for mail routes in reasonable quantity, which are absolute necessities at the pres-

ent time. Post offices costing $25,000 where the revenue is only $1,300 are absolutely and certainly not. They are luxuries. No, they are not even to be denominated luxuries; they are examples of wasteful extravagance. While hundreds and thousands of people living back in our country places are asking for weekly, tri-weekly and daily mail routes, in order that they may have the visit of the mail carrier and communication with others, allowing them to do their business, what is taking place under the management of this government? The revenues derived from the postal system of the country are being spent in unnecessary buildings, costing $25,000 and more so that there is not sufficient revenue to aid in the development of the mail carrying routes in order that the people in the distant parts of the country may have the visit of the postal carrier more frequently than they do to-day. Take that very instance and multiply it. You have to-day a surplus which goes into the postmaster's till of over $600,000. That surplus should be expended in giving mail service to the people in distant parts of the country, and if you go on erecting post offices out of it, instead of a surplus you will have an absolute deficit. By this means the earnings of the post office are robbed of their legitimate sphere which is to extend the postal facilities of the country. Such a system is not carried out in the United States or in Great Britain. The British post office could not exist for a single year if it undertook the policy of erecting post offices in towns of 1,300 inhabitants more or less. The British post office is managed to facilitate postal communications between the people and it is managed economically, and instead of $30,000 post offices scattered all through Great Britain and Ireland you have inexpensive and sufficient accommodation by rentals and the like. The United States is a rich country with a population of 90,000,000 and the United States is supposed to he very generous with the distribution of its money, but it does not pursue such a policy as is pursued in Canada. It places great post offices in great centres but in the smaller centres it goes on a less expensive plan. Its purpose is to increase the postal facilities for the people of the country. Why should Canada carry on this policy of robbing the post office revenue from its legitimate purpose of giving, more particularly, the people of the remote districts, to whom the arrival of the postman with a letter is a kind of benediction, far more frequent mail service than they have now. I do not make this protest in the hope that it will have any effect on the Minister of Public Works, but I do appeal to the business sense of this committee and I ask that before the vote is passed we shall have the opinion of the Postmaster General upon it.

It is wonderful how the views of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) have changed since he was a member of the government and since he undertook the construction of a public building in the town of Marysville, New Brunswick, where the Gibson Manufacturing Company have their establishment, and in the constituency which I think he then represented, but of that I am not sure. In these days my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) thought that was all right.
I rise to a point of order. I want to know what this has to do with the case?

I am replying to the argument of the hon. member (Mr. Foster) who has charged that we have engaged in a policy of extravagance and are depriving the postal revenue of certain of ns moneys, and I am showing that the policy we are now pursuing is that which he himself pursued when in office.
I rise to a point or order.
Don't you think the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) can take care of himself?

I will ask the chairman to take care of you just now. Assuming for the moment that what the Minister of Public Works says is true, what we are discussing just now is the extravagance of the government in regard to the item before the chair, and what the member for Toronto has done in the past can have no hearing on that question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has risen to a point of order, but what he is doing is discussing a point of ordel raised by another member. If he rises to a point of order he must state his point.
I am supporting the point of order raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell.)

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I realize that many of the arguments used and much of the debate is not strictly relevant, but I have hesitated to endeavour to draw the line closer because I believe the opposition are entitled to a large amount of latitude and to a large amount of information when the government asks for a vote. But, so far as the hon. minister has gone, while it did seem to me that it was some distance from this item, yet, he was entering into a question of comparison, and I think I am not called upon to stop him until his argument develops sufficiently to enable me to see whether his comparison is close enough to be relevant to the question before the chair.

I thought that were I able to auote the conduct of a gentleman so nrudent and so economical as my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) when he was Minister of Finance, as against his words now, it would be a strong argument to influence gentlemen on the other side. I thought I was making quite a strong point when 1 endeavoured to remind the committee that the hon. member (Mr. Foster) had justified in the strongest way the erection of a public building in Marysville, New Brunswick. which was not so important a town as Marieville, province of Quebec, in which we purpose erecting this building. But anart from that, I am quite prepared to justify the expenditure of a reasonable amount of public money in the construction of public buildings in the various towns and cities of the Dominion, and particularly so where it means the erection of onlv one public building in a county. It would seem to meet with the general approval of the House that it was not unreasonable to erect one building in the county town of a county, and Marieville is not only an important manufacturing and a growing town, but it is the county town of Rouville. With regard to the statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) that it is robbing the postal reveune, I sav it is nothing of the kind. There is not one dollar taken from the postal revenue in connection with the erection of this or anv other public building.
The Public Works Department pays not only for the buildings, but for the upkeep, the lighting, heating and all the cost of maintenance. Therefore the postal revenue in no way suffers. It is simply a question of policy whether or not we should erect public buildings where they .are reasonably required. My hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Wright) knows that he has made a demand that we should erect a public building in one of the towns of his constituency. I have not asked my colleagues to provide for it in the estimates this year, because we are spending public money in his constituency by building a much-needed wharf at the town of Gravenhurst, and I thought the matter of a public building might well stand over. My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson), who is always preaching economy, urged last year that we should erect a public building in the town of Milton, which is growing, and whose claims are no doubt worthy of consideration in the near future, and I do not think mv hon. friend would support my hon. friend from North Toronto in the statement he makes that this is evidence of extravagance and waste of public moneys. I think I can very well justify this expenditure. I do not think we should go to a greater expenditure than is reasonably necessary; but when a public building is Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
needed in this town, I think we can very well expend upon it between $20,000 and $25,000. It may be said that we could give a cheaper building. So we could; but the policy of the department is to erect buildings, whatever their size, of a substantial character, built of stone and brick, with solid foundations, and make them as fireproof as possible, so that they will last, and the cost of maintenance and repairs will be reduced to a minimum.
Has the site been purchased yet?
Yes, from the corporation, for the sum of $1,500.
Is the minister going to have space all around the building?
I think -we can do so in this case, as the lot is 64 feet by 132 feet.

The hon. minister has seen fit to refer to something which he alleges I said last year in support of his contention that a $25,000 post office should be erected in Marieville. If the minister will revise his recollection, he will remember that I stated that a gentleman who had been brought out from the city of Toronto, supported by the Minister of Agriculture, to contest a rural district, was the man who advocated a post office in the town of Milton and was going to have one if the people elected him. The people did not elect him, and the minister last year gave me to understand that the man had no promise from him of a post office in the town even if he had been elected. But, laying that aside, there is no comparison between the town of Milton and the village of Marieville either as to population or as to revenue. The revenue of the post office in Milton is about $4,000, that of Marieville about $1,300. True/ the hon. gentleman adds in the. surrounding country. If he did that in the case of Milton, he would get a population far in excess of that of Milton proper. This is a new departure; I think we had better stick by the old rule, when we want to know the requirements of a place, and take the population of the place itself without any reference to the suburbs. I would not have said anything on this matter if the hon. gentleman had not made a reference to the county I represent. I am not going to advocate a building, because if I did the minister would accuse me of being extravagant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then you do not want the building?

I am not going to say that. The people would like very much to have the building; they are entitled to lave it; but the disnosition of this government is not to give them the building. The

hon. gentleman talks about these two hat factories in Marieville. No doubt they are important industries, but right in the village of Acton there is one factory which alone employs about 300 people.
What do they make?

Leather. We have no customs house there, and the people want one badly. But this government is not disposed to accommodate the people. It would rather fritter away money on a small place where there are few people living and a comparatively small business is being done, than give accommodation where a large business is being done. Not many years ago-and the business has increased very rapidly since-the stationmaster told me that for that one firm there were sixty-eight carloads of raw material between Boston and Acton at the same time coming into their large manufactory. That gives you an idea of the extent of that factory, but the Minister of Customs has never given us a customs house. There is another institution there which requires the use of the customs house practically daily, yet this government does not think it worth while to give these people a customs officer or make that place a port or even an outport. If the government do not think it worth while to accommodate the people-and people supporting them too- where large business is being done, they will take the responsibility; and when the proper time comes, no doubt these people will get a customs house and a customs officer. But what I rose particularly to speak of was this. The Minister of Public Works became very jocular a short time ago in his reference to a place down in New Brunswick called Marysville. He accused my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) of having supported the erection of a building in that place and advanced that as an argument for the erection of this one. Well, I have some recollection of the discussion that took place on that item some fifteen or twenty years ago. The hon. gentleman was not here then but his friends were, and hour after hour-1 was almost going to say day after day-they used up the time of this House in denouncing the erection of that building. Yet now he makes use of that very structure as a justification for the erection of a building in this little town.
To meet the argument of the hon. member for North Toronto.

And a very logical argument it was! I wonder what his friends behind him thought of it True, I do not suppose there is a gentleman behind him who was in the House then, although pos-si'dv his colleague from Brome (Mr. Fisher) mav have been there. But as he was out
during one session, I am not sure that he either was present. I do not suppose there are more than eight or nine members in this House who were here then, and they have probably forgotten all about it. But I think the minister will admit that it was very illogical on his part to cite the erection of a public building in New Brunswick some fifteen or twenty years ago, which his friends then denounced as highly improper, as a justification for the erection of this one.
I did not say it was improper.
But his political friends denounced it for many hours as highly improper.

The hon. minister advances the argument that the parish of St. Marie, de Monnoir is also served by this post office. Well, St. Angele de Monnoir post office is onhr three and three-quarter miles from Marieville, and Rougemont is about four and seven-eighths miles from Marieville, and Richelieu four and a half miles, so that the place is pretty well surrounded by post offices and cannot give much postal revenue. But have tliey no rural mail delivery there?
I am told there is none.

The hon. minister has referred to my application a few years ago for a post office in one of the towns in my riding. I did press1 that matter very strongly on him. But as my riding gives a very large postal revenue, I thought that would entitle one of its towns to some consideration by this government. I was then met, however, by the same statement as that given to-night, namely, that on account of other public expenditure in that riding, the building of a post office could not be entertained. Two years ago there was an item to build a wharf in the district of Mus-koka and the government carried that estimate through but they never built the wharf. Last year they left that item out; and when, at the end of two years, I ask for a post office, I am met with the same reply that they are going to spend $4,000 in building a wharf there. Well, we have been now waiting three years for that wharf, and I shall have to go back and tell my people that, although they contribute to the revenue of this country $200,000 per annum, the government can give them neither a wharf nor a post office. It seems absurd that they should be so parsimonious with respect to that county and then spend $30,000 in Rouville in one year. I would not venture to ask the minister for a post office in my riding for a village which only gives the government a gross revenue of $1,300. We have plenty of villages in my constituency that size, but I would never

dream of asking for a post office at any one of them, but where we have a good large town with a good postal revenue, I am justified in asking for such an expenditure. I would not want a post office costing $25,000 to be built in a little village which gives only $1,300 gross revenue.

I want to call the attention of the House to the way in which the minister argues. I leave it to the chairman of the committee if I did not address myself to the question in point. I made two or three arguments, and the Minister of Public Works has never attempted to touch one of them. I asked him why, if Great Britain pursued a certain policy with regard to these general post offices, we should not carry out something like that policy here. I made another statement, that the United States does not indulge in this kind of expenditure, but carries on its post office in much more economical way by a system of rental and gives its great and widespread population all the advantages they require. It did seem to me that what was good policy for Great Britain and good policy for the United States in that respect might be good policy for Canada. Did the Minister of Public Works touch that argument? He did not. I used the other argument that there was a dissipation of the post office revenues in the construction of these public buildings, thereby reducing the surplus of the post office and preventing the furnishing of better postal facilities for the people. And how did the Minister of Public Works meet that argument? With a blank negative. He says: It is not true; my department pays all this expenditure. Why, the other night the minister led the House to believe that he paid his own laundry bills when travelling in an official car, but a question put to him later brought out the information that he put in his bills to the government-
The hon. member will excuse me; I did not make such a statement.
I find him figuring in the departmental accounts for large amounts for travelling expenses.
But the hon. member (Mr. Foster) said that I figured there for my laundry bills. I say that is absolutely untrue.	.
I am bound to accept the hon. minister's statement. But what 1 have said was the understanding in the House at that time, it seems to me.
No, it was not.

Of course, I accept the hon. gentleman's statement and do not pursue the subject further. But the hon. gentleman is absolutely wrong when he says Mr. WRIGHT.
that the post office does not suffer a diminution of its revenue by the building of twenty-five thousand dollar buildings in such places as Marieville. The moment you put up such a building in such a place, the surplus of the post office is reduced by added expense. For, when you have a twenty-five thousand dollar post office, you have to pay your postmaster and his assistants more salary. Other expenses also are increased. The result is that the post office itself is affected in its revenue by this drain. But what an argument for the Minister of Public Works, a grown man, to use in this committee-that his department pays for it! Whence comes the money to meet the expenditures of his department? Part of it comes from the revenues of the Post Office Department. There is a yearly surplus of something up to $1,000,000 which goes into the general fund into which flow all the revenues of Canada. Therefore every useless expense that the hon. minister nuts upon the country by paying $25,000 for a post office in a place with a population of 1,300 and with a revenue of $1,300 means just so much deducted from the revenues of the country and diminishes by that amount the possibility of a department like the Post Office extending its facilities as it otherwise might. Now, these are arguments addressed to the subject, and I call the attention of the committee to the way in which the minister does not meet them-or the way in which he thinks he meets them by going back twenty-five years or more to prove inconsistency on the part of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). The inconsistency of the member for North Toronto is not in question; the question before the committee is the proposed post office at Marieville. I have presented arguments on that subject and I believe they are good ones, but the minister slid around them on a side issue not touching one argument that I gave. I also put to him the question whether he did not think that, as this was an expenditure for the benefit of the Post Office Department, we should at least have the approval and request of the Postmaster General. Now, a new policy is laid down by the Minister of Public Works. It is that wherever you find a district with 1,300 people, having a village of about 1,300 more-
Seventeen hundred in 1907.

Well, give the minister the benefit of that-a district of 1,300 with a village of 1,700,-especially if it be a county town-you should spend $25,000 of the people's money in putting there a public building, no thought or question as to whether the public business requires that expenditure or not. But the moment you put up your building you saddle the country with an expenditure of 10 per cent annually for

depreciation, interest and so on. That is a charge forever upon the revenues of the country. Carry out this policy so that wherever you have this aggregation of 1,700 people with 1,300 around them and what is the result? Now, these, I think, were arguments, and the minister met them in his own peculiar way.

We have succeeded in getting quite a detailed description of the little village of Marieville which has been very interesting to me. I was glad to learn that it has manufactures, schools, churches and a population of 1,700. But the fact remains 1 that the total post office revenue of this flourishing village is less than $1,400. In the riding I have the honour to represent there are a number of prosperous, thriving villages, each with irs own churches, schools, manufactures, nice residences and so on, and each with a good country around it by including which you would have a population of 3,000 or 4,000. And in these places you have a post office revenue two or three times as much as that of Marieville. Yet these places never thought of asking this government to put up a $25,000 post office. I have no objection to this village, it being a county town, having a post office, but I do raise my protest against the spending of $25,000 to build a post office for a population of less than $2,000 and a revenue of less than $1,400. I consider it preposterous. If all the little villages and towns in the province of Ontario were to come down here thundering after the minister, and asking for post offices costing $25,000, places yielding a revenue twice the revenue of this little village, why, he would be overwhelmed. Now I enter my protest against the expenditure of $25,000 on a post office in a town of that size, with a revenue of less than $1,400. I can understand the minister wishing to build a post office there, but one costing $10,000 or $15,000 would be adequate. Why, we heard an hon. member of this House telling us last week of a town of 16,000 or 18,000 where the people were lined up outside waiting for their turn to enter and get their mail, and yet there is no effort to provide proper accommodation foil those people.

For several years in succession I have drawn attention to what I consider to be a growing abuse. We have now a good example of that abuse in this proposal to build a post office in a place where the revenue is only $1,300. I have taken the trouble to look over the government returns, and I have found several villages and towns in the section of the country that I am acquainted with that have no post office, and every one of them have a revenue much larger than Marieville. We have given Lake-field a very fine wharf.
But you have not given any public buildings?
We have just built a post office at Georgetown.
It is not so stated in the returns brought down by the government last year.
It has just been completed. We have also just completed a post office at Glencoe.

Probably, as in the case of Markham, it was put there in order to carry the riding. None of these places that I have mentioned have a post office, though every one of them has a much larger revenue than Marieville. Then go out to Lethbridge, where people are actually paying for the right of getting into the post office to get their letters, one in front of another, a large place with five times as much revenue as Marieville, and no effort is made to accommodate the public there. But when you come to this small village called Marieville with a revenue of $1,300, they must have a public building costing $25,000. Does not the minister think that is very unfair to these places with more business and of greater importance? I think it is unjustifiable, it is more, it is an absolute waste of public money. I venture to say that to-day, for fuel, lighting and so forth, we do not pay more than $175 a year; but after we have built this post office we will pay $400 to $600 for a man to take care of it, we will have to pay insurance, we will have to pay for reoairs, and then we will have to pay for fuel, wood and light in addition. Is that fair to other places with a much larger population and of greater importance? Is it a business way of spending the country's money? I say that no logical defence can be made on business

principles for spending this amount of money in Marieville.

I think I can present very good claims for a post office in my town of Aylmer. I was disappointed in looking over the estimates to find that the minister had not set aside something for a post office in Aylmer. I have taken the pains to look up some points where the government has given grants. Aylmer has 2,300 inhabitants, and the revenue from the post office is $6,000 or nearly $6,500. The following statement shows the expenditures that have been made by the government on post offices in other places:
