There are a number of small towns also in which grants have been made but there is only one town among fifteen in which the revenue is greater than in Aylmer. The customs collected at Port Burwell amounted, during the last fiscal year, to $100,000; at Port Stanley to $98,000 and at Aylmer to $10,000, making $208,000. I think I have established the claim of this place to a post office. I differ from some of my friends on this side of the House. I believe that the government is perfectly justified in spending money where it is needed.
I have not heard anybody on this side of the House object to that.

I do not think it is necessary to put large buildings and spend too much money, but I think I have established my claim for a post office at Aylmer. I have been in this House for four years and every year I have been trying to get a grant for a pos, office but I have not succeeded. I hope that when the Supplementary Estimates come down the minister will give us enough to start with.

My hon friend will find that in the estimates which are under consideration there are very few new items. There may be some exceptions to that but the great majority of the items asked for are in respect of public works which were in the estimates of two years ago. I think the claims of Aylmer, as presented to me now and as presented to me a year ago, Mr SPROULE.
are very strong and I beg to assure my hon. friend that they will have my most careful consideration. I am glad that my hon. friend takes such a reasonable view of this question. Without disparaging the view of hon. gentlemen opposite, because they have a perfect right to take any view that commends itself to their judgment, I must say that the view presented by the hon. gentleman is the only one which has been presented from that side of the House that appeals to my judgment. The hon. gentleman takes the correct view that it is not against the public interest to make reasonable expenditures for public buildings where these public buildings are reasonably and fairly required. I do not find that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) gets up and objects to the large expenditure in the city of Toronto. I do not suppose that the hon. gentleman who represents the city of Hamilton will object to the large expenditures in that city. But we ought not to forget that the small towns throughout the country are as much entitled to reasonable and fair consideration as these larger cities. If it were not for the people in the villages and small towns these large cities would not be as prosperous as they are to-day. They are fed by the rural districts and the small towns and villages. We are not expending upon all these small buildings in all the small towns and cities as much in one year as we sometimes spend upon ong of these large cities such as Montreal and Toronto. Therefore, I think the request that is made by the hon. member for a reasonable recognition of the claims of the smaller cities and towns throughout the country is fair and just, and it will afford me very great pleasure as Minister of Public Works to recognize these claims when they are fairly presented to the House as they have been presented to me this evening by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat.

The question is all in the use of the word 'reasonable.' There has been no gentleman on this side of the House, that 1 have ever heard, object to any reasonable expenditure, but when the minister is satisfied to claim that a $25,000 post office in a little two by four village-
A growing town.

A little two by four village-that is all it is. I have half a dozen towns in the riding that I have the honour to represent larger than this and I would not insult the intelligence of the people of my riding or the House of Commons by coming here and asking for post offices to be scattered around like this. An ordinary building is ample in any one of these villages to accommodate the public as far as the post office is concerned. Twenty-five thousand dollars for a post office in a little

"two by four town like Marieville is unreasonable and therefore the minister's argument does not hold good.

The minister advances the argument that many of these estimates were put in two years ago. They were just as unjustifiable then as they are to-day. Why were they put in? When there was an election coming on the estimates were padded by these large proposed expenditures and then after the election was over they were allowed to drop and the government did not go on with the expenditure. The minister advances that as a justification for voting this money now and going on with the expenditure. That is one line -of defence. Another is that these small places are entitled to expenditure. I do not think his argument is worthy of the consideration of any intelligent man in this House. The first consideration that ought to engage the attention of this House is: What is required for the accommodation and service of the public? Where you can get a building for a rent that will be very much less than the interest upon the money which would build another suitable for the accommodation of the people, you are not justified in spending the money upon a public building. But if we are told that this is for the accommodation of the public, why not accommodate Lethbridge where there is such a large return?
We are going to accommodate Lethbridge.

This has been going on for two or three years and a most urgent appeal has been made by the member for the constituency but it has fallen upon deaf ears. We are not here for the purpose of distributing money over the country for the sake of making an expenditure where it is not needed. That should not be the aim of parliament. Therefore there is no force in the argument of the minister. Nor, is there any cogency in the argument, that because the estimates were padded two years ago in anticipation of an election we must carry them out in some cases while in other cases they must be dropped. We must be guided by the requirements of the public. If the public can be accommodated at a less expenditure to the country than by putting up a public building it should be done in that way. If you are justified in expending money in a small place like that in the province of Quebec, by the same parity of reasoning you are justified in spending public money in every similar small place in every province of the Dominion.
It was thought originally that this post office would be constructed for $5,800.
I never made that statement.
There was $5,800 orig-nally voted.
That was only to begin.

There is nothing in the vote to show that it was only to begin, and when your estimates contain no explanation it is reasonable to suppose that the vote would cover the cost of the building. On behalf of the people in my county I protest against the squandering of money in this way. Last year I went to the Postmaster General with petitions from residents in different parts of Frontenac asking for better mail facilities. In one of the oldest settlements in the province of Ontario about ten miles from the city of Kingston, the residents have a -mail service three times a week and for years they have been asking for a daily mail service the extra cost of which would amount to only $50 a year, and when I presented that petition to the Postmaster General I was told that the government did not have the money to spare for that. In another part of my county the nearest post office is five miles away from the nearest of the residents and seven miles distant on the average and they have been asking not for a daily mail service but simply begging and praying for post office facilities and a mail twice a week, and the minister has told me that they have no money for that purpose. There are many like instances in the county of Frontenac and I presume in other counties throughout the Dominion where the people in the rural communities are suffering for lack of proper mail facilities. The Minister of Public Works has laid down a new doctrine to-night and one which may give some light to the people of my county, when he told a gentleman on this side of the House that the reason they did not erect a public building in a large town in his riding was because they spent iome money on the harbour in that constituency. I suppose then that the people of Frontenac are to take it for granted that the reason they have to walk seven miles for their mail is because nearly $100,000 was spent on providing residences at Kingston for men drawing a salary of $400 a year. I suppose, had the member for Frontenac asked some years ago for better postal facilities, he would have been told that the government had already spent a large amount of money in that county for erecting stables for the military college, which, although erected five years ago have never had a horse inside of them yet. That is the way the money of the people is squandered.
Is Kingston in the hon. gentleman's constituency?

Kingston is not in the hon. gentleman's constituency, but it is in

the county of Frontenac and these stables are in Barriefield which is in my constituency, and I suppose because they have been erected in Barriefield and the money expended in the county, that is the reason why people in the county of Frontenac have to walk seven or eight miles to get their mail, although my constituents have not got any benefit from these stables, nor have the soldiers either.
Nor the horses.
I made no statement such as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards) attributes to me.

The minister gave as an excuse for not erecting a post office in a certain place where the revenue was far greater than it is in Marieville that the government had spent money in erecting other works in the constituency.
The hon. gentleman is speaking of rural mail delivery.

I did not mention rural mail delivery to-night and the Minister of Public Works must be dreaming if he thinks I did. I am referring to the fact that there are people in my county who are not asking for rural mail delivery but who have to walk seven and eight miles to get their letters and who want a post office placed in their midst.
Has the hon. gentleman pressed for the erection of a post office building in his constituency?
Of a $25,000 building?
Of any building?
No, I have not.
What does the hon. gentleman complain about?

I am not responsible for your understanding if I cannot make it clear to you. What we ask is that you allow some person in that neighbourhood to keep a post office in his house so that the people will not have to travel seven or eight miles to get their letters. Does the minister understand now what I am talking about? To bring this matter to a head, and believing this vote is not a reasonable one I move that this item be reduced by $6,500.

It seems to me that the hon. gentleman has not given any reason whv this item should be reduced. Marieville is a progressive town, factories have been recently erected there and a large number of people employed.
According to the figures the minister gave us, it has only grown during the last six years at the rate of fifty a year.
It has increased from 1,300 to 1,600.
The minister has spoken of the population being up to 1,700. What authority has he for making that statement?

There was a census taken by the municipal authorities in 1907, and the population was then 1,671. It is estimated that now, including the students and attendants at the college, there is in the town of Marieville alone a population of 2,000, while if you add to that the population of the parish which immediately surrounds the town, you will have a population of about 3,000 people who will be accommodated by that public building. If we are going to erect a substantial building, I do not see how we can do it for much less than the amount named. Therefore, I hope the committee will see that it would not be reasonable to support the amendment of the hon. member for Frontenac.
Amendment negatived.
Megantic public building-revote of $4,900 lapsed, $10,000.
What is the population and revenue?
The population is nearly 2,000.
What about the site?
It has been purchased at $4,000.
When was it purchased?
In January, 1907, from the Presbyterian congregation. The postal re venue is $2,637 and the customs revenue $10,777.
What is the estimated cost?

$25,000, including the site, heating and everything.
Montreal general post office-enlargement and alterations, $80,000.

This is for completion of the work which has been under contract. We are obliged to make considerable alterations to the old building so as to make it in harmony with the new building and more fireproof.
Is this intended to finish the work there?
No.
How much will be required?

That depends on what we do. If we make the old building fireproof, it is going to cost considerably more.

There is a strong inducement to do so, as we have made the new building fireproof.
Should not the minister have his mind made up as to what he is going to do before he comes and asks for a vote?

What we are asking for will iust about complete the payments on the present contract. If we go on and remodel the old building and make it fireproof we shall have to come to parliament for another vote.

It is an insult to the intelligence of the people's representatives for ministers of the Crown to ask them to vote public money without giving them the information they are entitled to have. Twenty-five years ago the minister of the Crown would be shamed out of this House if he could not give more information than the hon. gentleman has given us to-night.
I have a great deal.

If the hon. minister has, he manages to keep it to himself most sedulously. He thinks he can jolly the House along without giving any information, and it is often to my mind a question whether he really desires to give the information even when he has it, and whether he does not think it infra dig to give information to members of the opposition. That conduct has so often shocked my sense of right that I cannot refrain from giving expression to my opinion concerning it.
The trouble with my hon. friend is that he gets unduly excited, What information does he desire with regard to this post office building?

I want to know how much we are committing ourselves to in the expenditure on this undertaking, what will it cost when completed, what is the outline of the building we propose to erect, is it fireproof, is it of wood, stone or brick, and will it give the service required? If contracts have been let, have they been let by tender and has the lowest tender been accepted? If plans have been made out. what do they show? He says that I am unduly excited. Has he ever sat in this House and heard the right hon. the Prime Minister explain his estimates. I never saw an occasion on which that right hon. gentleman had any trouble with them. Why? Because he is perfectly frank and candid and courteous, and when asked a question immediately answers, and shows no desire to jolly the House along or keep back information. How is it that it takes the Minister of Public Works so much longer to get his estimates through than the Prime Minister? Because the Prime Minister, and I may say the same of several
others, shows a desire to give all the information he can without reserve.

As the hon. gentleman is an old member, I cannot allow to pass certain remarks and innuendos made by him without some reply, especially when he uses language so unparliamentary as to say that I am seeking to jolly the committee. When he does so, he shows that he has but a slight appreciation of the meaning of words.
What I said was that that was the impression left on my mind and what appeared to be the disposition of the hon. gentleman.

Not .being able to look into the mind of my hon. friend to see what kind of a mind it is, I cannot know what gives him the impression of an attempt on my part to jolly the House. I have no desire to jolly the hon. member or any member of the committee. It is impossible for him to point to a single instance in which I refused to give all the information possible. He ought to bear in mind that there are some twelve hundred items in the estimates. I cannot keep them all in mind, but have to rely on my chief architect and my deputy and the memoranda I have for the information asked. On reflection my hon. friend will see that it was very unfair on his part to pass these reflections without asking a single question.
Did I not ask the hon. minister what he proposed to do with the $80,000?

I said I was considering the question of making that building fireproof and then said that this amount would just about cover the contract now had with Lyall and Sons. He asks why I did not tell him whether this contract was let after tender or not. Well, two years ago we made the contract for that building, and I then told him we would spend this whole sum on the building as then contemplated, but that if we decided to make it fireproof we would have to ask for a further vote. I think he will see on reflection that he does- me a great injustice. I trust that he will let the item pass, and when he wants information be good enough to ask for it.
Who was the contractor?
Lyall and Sons.
What contracts have they with the government other than this?
First, the main contract which was for rebuilding the new part, then the heating apparatus. The electric wiring was given to Dawson & Company, Limited, of Montreal.
The hon. minister says I did not ask him a question. I asked him specifically whether this was all _ the expenditure that would be required, or whether he would require any more.
I said that if we decided to make the building fireproof we would require to ask for more.

I would suppose that *before undertaking the expenditure of money the minister would have made some calculation and be able to give the House some information as to what this building will cost the country when completed. He replied that would depend on whether more expenditure would be made after this vote. In seven cases out of ten when I put him a question, the minister will turn to something else and try to divert attention and apparently does not desire to answer frankly.
Oh, no.

I have seen other Ministers of Public Works, I have seen Sir Hector Langevin, when Minister of Public Works, stand for hours with his book in his hand and his deputy beside him, and give all information regarding the item under discussion in advance without waiting to be asked. If anything were neglected or forgotten in his memo, he would ask his deputy. Sir Richard Cartwright, when he was in this House, did the same.
An ho'n. MEMBER. And the Minister of Agriculture.
The only trouble with him is that he is so anxious to give information that a few questions will keep him going all night.
Has this firm any other contracts with the Public Works Department in any other part of Canada?
No, no other.
What is the amount of the contracts let?
For the addition to the main building, $487,527; heating apparatus, $18,407; electric wiring and fittings, $6,392.46.	i
To whom are they let?

For the addition to the building and for the heating, Messrs. P. Lyall & Sons, and for the electric wiring and fittings, Dawson & Co., Ltd.
Montreal-new postal station ' D/ at Point St. Charles, $6,000.
I submit, we have done a pretty fair day's work, and the minister should let us go.
We ought to finish up Quebec; we have only a few items.
We are only about half through.
Finish Montreal.

This $6,000 will complete this new building.
Plessisville public building, $2,000.
What is the population of Plessisville?
In 1901 it was 1,586.
In what county is it?
In Megantic. This amount will complete the building. It is under contract.

I do not think it fair to go on with the succeeding items, foT they are for buildings for militia purposes, and the Minister of Militia is not here. He ought to be here when these items are under consideration.
I'll tejl you what we might do,-let us pass over these votes for military buildings and take the next five small items.
There are members from Quebec who are not present, and I think these items should be left over.
We had better take the item for Roberval.
No matter when a suggestion is made to stop, the hon. minister always has three or four more items that he wants to put through.
I have left over these military items. We might take Roberval.
No, Mr. Chairman. I think it time to close the House. I do not want to be over anxious, but I think it only fair to the committee that proceedings should close.
We get along better if, when we have done a reasonable day's work, we stop.

I should be sorry to keep my hon. friends here too late.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?
